#6385. What keeps people recycling for decades? One town offers clues

A Japanese study found that stronger neighborhood ties and wider social connections were linked to higher recycling participation.

Most recycling programs demand the same daily effort for years to come. They need rules and bins to get off the ground, but the factors that keep people sorting after decades have received less attention.

Osaki, a town in southern Japan, offers a test case. Residents have sorted their trash for more than 20 years, and the town has one of the country’s highest recycling rates.

A new survey found that residents who reported closer ties with their neighbors also reported more waste sorting and more help for others at collection points.

They also reported more positive views of recycling as well as feeling that family and neighbors would expect them to recycle.

Naoko Kaida, a professor at the University of Tsukuba, led the study with colleagues.

The small town of Osaki was running low on landfill space by the late 1990s.

Businesses, residents, and the local government worked together to keep as much waste as possible out of the landfill.

Residents sort their waste into 28 categories including cans, plastic bottles, plastic packaging, cardboard, and even diapers. They separate other bottles by color.

Residents take their sorted waste to shared community recycling stations managed by local hygiene associations. In many communities, residents oversee the sorting themselves.

The effort has worked, sharply reducing the town’s reliance on landfills. Since 2006, over 80% of the waste generated in Osaki has gone to recycling.

Previous studies tried to clarify the relation between recycling and social ties.

Few studies, however, have examined these relationships in a place where waste sorting has become routine. Osaki began with 16 sorting categories in 2000 and later expanded to 28.

Kaida works at the Institute of Systems and Information Engineering, University of Tsukuba, and her team mailed the anonymous questionnaire to all 5,773 households in Osaki in late 2024. Any adult living in one of the households could fill out the questionnaire.

Of the 805 questionnaires returned over four weeks, 277 were complete enough to analyze.

A number of the questions focused on the residents’ perception of their neighbors in terms of the degree of trust they inspired, how well they knew them, and how sure the residents were that their neighbors would help in the case of a disaster.

The questions on social relationships other than those with close neighbors covered people with whom residents shared hobbies, friends with whom they kept in touch although they lived far away, and trusted contacts at the workplace or at school.

Social scientists call both kinds of relationship social capital.

On a six-point scale, residents rated their waste handling on average at 5.36 for following the rules and 4.11 for helping others at the waste sorting stations.

The first score covered all 28 sorting categories and labeling garbage bags, while the second covered unloading garbage and helping people unsure how to sort it.

The team refers to a model of behavior that psychologists frequently use.

According to this model, a person’s intention to behave in a certain way depends on their attitudes to the behavior, other people’s expectations, and their capacity to behave in the intended way.

First, residents who reported stronger neighborhood ties felt more positive about the sorting of waste, and felt more strongly that their family and their neighbors expected them to follow the rules and recycle.

These views in turn were associated with an intention to continue sorting waste, which Kaida and her team found to be the best predictor of the recycling behavior residents reported.

The relationship between neighborhood ties and sorting behavior was indirect, through attitudes and expectations, with no direct link between the two in the team’s model.

Of the three factors in the model, attitude had the strongest tie to intention, which the authors suggested could reflect decades of town policy promoting waste sorting and its benefits.

Social connections outside the neighborhood, such as friendships and hobby groups, were directly linked to recycling and helping others at the station.

This link was about as strong as the indirect link between neighborhood relationships and these behaviors.

The authors suggested, however, that outside contacts may be sources of information or even of resources which can help residents learn and keep up with a very complicated system such as that of waste sorting in Osaki.

In the model, these wider ties had no clear link to residents’ attitudes, their sense of others’ expectations or how capable they felt.

Both kinds of relationship were associated with higher levels of recycling behavior but only to a small degree.

Neither type of social connection was clearly linked to how confident residents felt about their ability to recycle.

The researchers suggested that this confidence may depend more on clear rules, available facilities, and years of recycling experience.

Osaki is an aging town with about 11,700 inhabitants and an average age of 53 in 2020, part of the wider pattern of shrinking, aging populations in rural Japan.

Older residents reported stronger neighborly ties and felt more expectation from others, but the relationship between social ties and recycling behavior remained after controlling for age.

This one-time survey can only report on correlation, meaning that it can show a link between close neighbors and recycling but cannot tell us whether one causes the other.

One point for future studies is to measure social ties and recycling attitudes over time to see how they change together.

The 277 respondents were an older group. About half of them were in their 60s or 70s, and only five respondents were in their 20s.

As mentioned earlier, the same residents rated their recycling behavior, and the researchers did not watch them sort.

Osaki’s established sorting system and neighborhood involvement may limit how well the findings apply elsewhere.

The authors suggested that the same type of relationships may exist in other localities where residents of the neighborhoods help manage waste collection.

In contrast to the rural settings of many Japanese towns, however, community ties in the cities are generally looser, and the link may be weaker.

Very close ties to neighbors, however, carry risks too, the authors wrote, as residents can perceive pressure to conform or find themselves excluded when neighbors monitor one another.

The researchers suggested that towns should do more than share information and enforce recycling rules to keep recycling rates high.

They should also organize regular activities that bring neighbors together and encourage younger generations to recycle.

How much these ties matter likely depends on how a town organizes its waste collection, which future studies comparing towns with different waste sorting systems could clarify.

The full study was published in the Journal of Material Cycles and Waste Management.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope could capture images 30% sharper than — and remain operational for twice as long as — initially expected. Researchers say these "remarkable" developments could greatly enhance the volume and quality of the data they will analyze.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is nearing its final destination more than 1 million miles (1.6 million kilometers) from Earth, where it will soon scour the universe for a host of cosmological treasures, including an estimated 100,000 new alien worlds.

But even before its mission truly begins, recent developments suggest the state-of-the-art spacecraft could take better images than — and remain operational for more than twice as long as — initially expected, further delighting already-excited astronomers.

"It is fantastic to learn that Roman is not just reaching its design goals but exceeding them," Eamonn Kerins, an astronomer at the University of Manchester in the U.K. who will help lead one of Roman's major surveys, told Live Science.

Roman is NASA's latest flagship space telescope, following in the footsteps of iconic observatories like the Hubble Space Telescope and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The $4 billion machine ‪—‬ which is over 42 feet (12.7 meters) long and weighs around the same as a fully grown Tyrannosaurus rex ‪—‬ successfully launched into space on Aug. 30, more than a decade after scientists started building it.

The telescope is now en route to Lagrange point 2 (L2), a fixed point relative to our planet where Earth's gravity and the sun's gravity cancel each other out. There, Roman will join several other important spacecraft, including JWST and the European Space Agency's Euclid telescope.

Roman was launched into space on board one of SpaceX's Falcon heavy rockets. It lifted off Aug. 30 from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

During Roman's journey to L2, which is currently around 85% complete, mission scientists have remotely switched on the telescope's various instruments to test whether they function as expected. So far, this "commissioning process" has gone off without a hitch, and by the time Roman arrives in less than two weeks, it should be ready to snap its first in-depth images of the cosmos.

Researchers were already pumped to see what Roman will be able to do once it is in place and fully switched on. However, that excitement has further intensified in recent weeks, thanks to two postlaunch developments.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

First, a series of near-perfect rocket burns, executed during and shortly after launch, saved more than a decade's worth of fuel that can now be used to extend Roman's mission. Second, after remotely adjusting the telescope's mirror, researchers discovered it should be capable of snapping images with around 30% greater detail than engineers predicted.

The team that designed, launched and remotely commissioned the orbital observatory has "done an amazing job" and "their work has ensured that Roman is more than up to the task," Kerins said.

Shortly after Roman arrived in space on board a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket that lifted off from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida, mission scientists conducted two major burns, or engine firings, which gave the spacecraft enough momentum to escape Earth's orbit and make the journey to L2.

Roman is around the same size as a small truck and was packed into the nose cone of the Falcon Heavy rocket prior to launch.

Thanks to a combination of "exquisite planning by our orbital dynamics team" and "brilliant execution by the operations team," these burns were so precise that each one saved up to four years' worth of fuel, Jamie Dunn, director of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, said in a Sept. 14 statement.

On top of this, Roman ended up being much lighter than initially planned, which allowed engineers to pack another four years' worth of fuel into the spacecraft before launch. "Since Roman's [weight] was lower than we budgeted for, we were able to fill the propellant tanks to their capacity rather than only filling them as much as we needed," Alison Rao, the Roman propulsion lead at NASA Goddard, said in the statement.

In total, these savings could give Roman an additional 12 years of fuel, which could more than double the mission's planned 10-year lifespan. That means Roman could still be capturing images of the cosmos in 2048.

Given that Roman can collect data up to 1,000 times faster than Hubble, this extended lifespan will greatly enhance the amount of data the new space telescope will be able to capture. "With a 20-year Roman lifetime, we could, in theory, do over 20,000 years of Hubble survey work," Kerins said. "That's a lot of science!"

Roman is now on its way to L2, where the gravity of Earth and the sun cancel out, allowing it to remain in one place without expending much fuel.

This prolonged lifespan will let astronomers compare images of specific objects decades apart — such as expanding nebulas or colliding galaxies — allowing them to detect changes they otherwise might have missed.

It may also let them study objects or phenomena that we haven't even discovered yet, which is particularly exciting, Kerins noted. "The real show-stopper results will be new things we just aren't even thinking about right now," he said. "The possibilities are truly breathtaking."

There is also the chance that Roman's mission could be extended even further, because engineers often find clever ways of making active spacecraft last longer. For example, Hubble is more than two decades past its initial mission parameters, and the recently deceased Swift Observatory lasted 10 times longer than initially predicted before falling back to Earth last week.

Roman's secret weapon is arguably its Wide Field Instrument (WFI), made up of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror, which will capture ultra-detailed images with a field of view roughly 100 times larger than Hubble's.

Roman's WFI consists of a 288-megapixel camera attached to a 7.9-foot (2.4 m) mirror. It will be capable of capturing images with a field of view 100 times greater than Hubble.

We have already seen the first WFI images — a series of blurry, green dots captured during a test of the instrument's 18 different light detectors ( see below). However, those photos were nothing like what WFI will capture in the future; those images will be so detailed that you would need dozens of high-definition TVs to properly display a single snap in full resolution, Kerins said.

After Roman completes the initial WFI commissioning phase, those images will be around 30% sharper than designers predicted. "All of the images from Roman's cosmic surveys will be even sharper than we expected," Alden Jurling, a senior optical engineer who works on Roman at NASA Goddard, said in an Oct. 14 statement. "It's a great outcome."

The improvements were first noticed after the WFI's car-sized mirror was realigned by just one-sixteenth the diameter of a human hair, demonstrating just how intricate the commissioning process has been. "Calibrating an instrument is like tuning a piano or guitar before a concert," Maxime Rizzo, a WFI systems engineer at NASA Goddard, said in the statement. "You adjust everything until it's just how you want it and then leave the settings alone so it performs consistently while you use it."

NASA released Roman's first photos on Sept. 15. Each small square represents one of the telescope's light detectors, and each blurry green spot is a distant star. (This is just a test image and does not represent how the telescope's proper photos will look.)

The improved image quality could really come to the fore during Roman's hunt for potentially habitable exoplanets, which is what Live Science's readers are most excited about for this mission.

Kerins, who is leading the Exoplanet Demographics Working Group for the Transits in the Roman Exoplanets Survey, is particularly excited about this development, but he said it does not necessarily guarantee that Roman will find more exoplanets than initially predicted.

The rest of Roman's commissioning phase is also proceeding as planned.

Roman's coronagraph instrument, which will block out the light from distant stars to allow WFI to spot alien worlds, has passed its main commissioning phase and is working as intended, according to a NASA blog post.

Roman has completed around 85% of its journey to L2 and should arrive at its final destination in the next few weeks. (The timeline in this image is a screenshot from Roman's commissioning process website, captured on Nov. 11.)

Meanwhile, a global network of ground stations, which will receive up to 1.4 terabytes of data from Roman every day, has established contact with the spacecraft and is receiving signals as expected, another blog post revealed.

All of these early wins raise hopes that Roman can have a long and successful career, and are a testament to the years of work that went into designing the spacecraft and planning the mission.

"What we're seeing now with the actual optical performance and estimated lifetime of Roman is just how good that design process has been," Kerins said. "It's a remarkable achievement. I can't wait to see what Roman is going to give us."

Harry is a U.K.-based senior staff writer at Live Science. He studied marine biology at the University of Exeter before training to become a journalist. He covers a wide range of topics including space exploration, planetary science, space weather, climate change, animal behavior and paleontology. His recent work on the solar maximum won "best space submission" at the 2024 Aerospace Media Awards and was shortlisted in the "top scoop" category at the NCTJ Awards for Excellence in 2023. He also writes Live Science's weekly Earth from space series.

#6383. Early humans may have kept souvenirs half a million years ago

Early humans may have collected keepsakes 500,000 years ago, a habit researchers suggest could have helped shape memory and a sense of self.

Somewhere in your house there’s a stone from a beach. A shell from a holiday. A pinecone your kid picked up on a walk three years ago that you can’t bring yourself to throw away.

It does nothing but it means everything. And according to a new study, you’re not the first human to feel that way. Not by about half a million years.

The study was led by Ran Barkai and Yoav Ram at Tel Aviv University.

The team argues that early humans in the Levant were already picking up colorful pebbles, fossil-studded rocks, and old weathered tools and carrying them home for reasons that may have gone beyond practical use.

According to the scientists, the habit of anchoring memories to objects didn’t just reflect the human mind. It may have helped build it.

The most striking evidence comes from the Sakhnin Valley in Lower Galilee.

Out of more than 200 surveyed handaxes at this Acheulean landscape, roughly ten were shaped around fossil imprints or unusual geological formations embedded in flint nodules.

Those nodules were harder to knap. Toolmakers normally avoided them.

But someone chose them anyway, then went out of their way to position the fossil or geological oddity at the center of the tool’s face.

The researchers argue that these choices were deliberate.

At Qesem Cave, small round colorful pebbles showed up starting around 400,000 years ago and kept showing up for the next 200,000 years. Their practical purpose remains unclear.

Then there’s something stranger. At Revadim, Jaljulia, and Qesem Cave, people picked up old flint tools that had been lying in the landscape long enough to develop a visible patina.

They resharpened the cutting edges, but they kept the old surfaces: the scars, the color changes, the story written into the stone.

Under magnification, wear traces show these recycled tools were barely used in their second life.

The fresh edges made them functional; preserving the patina may have held personal meaning.

The researchers call them “memory objects.”

Most discussions of weird prehistoric objects land on the same explanations. Art. Ritual. Status symbols. Shared cultural meaning.

This study does something different. It argues these objects worked at the personal level first.

No audience was required and no shared convention needed. Just one person who remembers what the stone means.

The authors lay out four things that separate a souvenir from a decoration: it’s tied to a specific episode in someone’s life, it helps verify a real experience against an imagined one, keeping it takes deliberate effort, and its meaning is private.

That last part matters. A keepsake points to something that happened to you, and only you need to know its meaning.

So how does holding a rock help you remember? The mechanism the authors point to is source monitoring. That refers to the brain’s way of sorting real experiences from dreams, hearsay, and imagination.

The hippocampus reconstructs episodes from partial cues. The perirhinal cortex handles familiarity, and the parahippocampal cortex fills in contextual detail.

The authors propose that a keepsake’s physical features could engage these memory systems together.

That matters more than it sounds. In small societies built on reciprocity, people who could reliably distinguish real experiences from imagined ones may have had an advantage.

Over enough generations, routine souvenir-keeping may have created a “souvenir niche” that favored brains better wired for autobiographical memory and sense of self.

“The disappearance of large animals, particularly elephants, required early humans to develop new hunting methods and become familiar with hunting grounds inhabited by animals such as fallow deer and wild cattle,” Barkai said.

“Objects taken from these places may have helped them maintain a personal connection with the places that would henceforth provide their livelihood.”

The elephant vanished from the Levant around 400,000 years ago. So did Homo erectus and  the Acheulean tool tradition.

Everything shifted. Smaller, faster prey meant learning new territories from scratch.

Familiar landscapes couldn’t be taken for granted anymore. Portable pieces of those places became worth carrying home.

The authors are clear this isn’t proof. Not every odd stone was a keepsake.

But the pattern is there. Objects with no clear practical role were carried far from their source, curated over long use-lives, and found near hearths and living areas rather than tool-making debris.

Aesthetics and raw material shortage don’t explain it cleanly.

“When early humans brought a colorful stone or an old tool they had found in the landscape back to their cave, that object may have helped them remember a significant event or encounter for the rest of their lives,” Ram said.

“In this way, keepsakes may have become a kind of ‘external memory device,’ supporting the evolution of brain mechanisms responsible for autobiographical memory, which is so characteristic of us as humans and so important in shaping our identity.”

The study is published in the journal Evolutionary Anthropology.

#6382. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

Questions or comments on this article? E-mail us at feedback@sciencenews.org | Reprints FAQ

K.R. Tuttle et al. Effects of semaglutide on kidney disease in type 2 diabetes: a randomized placebo-controlled trial. Nature Medicine. 2026. doi: 10.1038/s41591-026-04674-2

V. Perkovic et al. Effects of semaglutide on chronic kidney disease in patients with type 2 diabetes. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. doi: 10.1056/NEJMoa2403347

#6381. Laser scanner that maps the chemistry inside tissue samples has been miniaturized into a handheld portable device

A handheld probe maps tissue chemistry without stains, and in lab tests its images closely matched those from a full-size instrument.

Machines that can map the chemistry inside a slice of tissue, showing where proteins and fats sit without using dye, have been too big to leave the lab bench.

A research team has now modified the imaging head of one to fit a probe that is 8 inches (20 centimeters) long. In side-by-side tests, its pictures closely matched those from a full-size lab instrument.

That matters because full-size machines can’t be carried to where patients are. A probe this size could someday work in the room where a tumor is removed.

So far, though, it has only tested the chemistry in thin slices of preserved tissue and plastics.

The work was done in Rohith Reddy’s lab at the University of Houston, and a pathologist at MD Anderson Cancer Center supplied bone marrow samples. Reddy already has a use in mind.

“Ultimately, this technology could make it possible to assess tissue during cancer surgery,” said Reddy, who leads the team. “After removing a suspected tumor, a surgeon could scan the freshly excised tissue.”

This would “help determine whether it is malignant or whether cancer cells remain at the surgical margin. This complementary information would be available while the patient is still in the operating room instead of having to wait for results from laboratory testing,” Reddy explained.

The instrument works with mid-infrared light. Like all infrared light, it’s invisible, and its waves are longer than the ones a TV remote sends. Molecules absorb this light at wavelengths set by the bonds holding their atoms together. That gives proteins, fats and DNA each a pattern of their own.

The system uses two lasers aimed at the same tiny spot. One sends mid-infrared light in bursts, 1,000 times a second. Where molecules in the spot absorb it, the spot warms very slightly. A second laser, a red one, picks up the small changes that the warming causes.

Sweep that spot across a sample, point by point, and the result is a map of where a chosen chemical sits. Because visible red light does the detecting, the map shows tissue chemistry detail finer than a single cell.

No stain is needed. Pathology labs normally dye tissue before anyone looks at it, and dyes are often impractical outside the lab because of toxicity, regulation and cost, the team wrote.

Shrinking the machine meant solving one stubborn problem. The red light and the mid-infrared light have to land on exactly the same point. However, lens materials that work well for one tend to work badly for the other.

Materials that pass red light often absorb mid-infrared, while ones built for mid-infrared can bend different colors by different amounts and blur the signal.

Reddy’s team sent the infrared light through a special glass fiber made for those wavelengths, which did away with bulky open-air optics.

They also swapped lenses for mirrors, since a mirror reflects both kinds of light. A curved mirror at the tip focuses both beams onto one spot.

“Careful optical design and alignment helped to minimize the image distortions that mirrors can cause. We also designed the handheld scanner to connect to the light source through a fiber-optic cable, allowing it to be maneuvered easily around a sample,” Reddy said.

The lasers and electronics sit in a base unit of less than 1.5 square feet (0.14 square meters). Commercial instruments of this kind take up more than 9 square feet (0.84 square meters) of optical table, more than a card table’s top.

The team first scanned a test chart patterned onto a crystal slide. The handheld system picked out details about 0.00008 inches (2 micrometers) across. Its images of the chart closely matched a commercial benchtop instrument’s.

Next came human tissue: thin slices of cervical cancer from two patients and ovarian cancer from two others.

Images from the handheld probe and the benchtop machine correlated at 0.90, compared at a coarse level of detail, on a scale where 1 would be a perfect match.

In ovarian cancer tissue, the tissue chemistry patterns it recorded agreed with a standard lab infrared measurement at 0.935 on a similar scale.

In plain terms, the small probe recorded close to what the big machines did. Its scans also lined up with dyed slices of the same tissue, the kind that pathologists read every day. Connective tissue that the dye highlighted showed up strongly in the undyed chemical image.

A bone marrow biopsy from a patient gave a harder test. Doctors check marrow for a buildup of collagen, a kind of scarring linked to the marrow making fewer blood cells. They usually spot it with a stain that turns collagen blue.

Without any stain, the chemical scan picked out the dense framework of bone in the sample. It also showed the collagen wrapped around a blood vessel, matching the blue in a stained slice next to it.

The team tried a second scanning style on mouse kidney tissue, with the mirror at the tip both turning and moving. That scan showed a glomerulus, one of the kidney’s tiny filters, along with chemical detail that a plain image from the red laser alone didn’t have.

Every sample was a thin, preserved slice on a slide. The team hasn’t imaged living tissue, and none of the samples was fresh from surgery, which is the setting Reddy described.

“Although the current platform is still a research prototype, it establishes a technical foundation for field-deployable, label-free chemical imaging,” Reddy said.

The probe also used only part of the range its laser can reach. That laser is built from four chips that point in slightly different directions, so crossing from one chip to the next meant realigning the light into the fiber by hand.

In these tests, a moving mirror inside the probe or a stage that shifted the sample did the scanning.

The team hasn’t yet tested whether these scans can help a doctor tell cancer from healthy tissue. The researchers plan to widen the range of infrared light the probe uses and to speed up scanning, which would make holding it freehand more practical.

Before any clinical use, its repeatability, safety and diagnostic performance still have to be tested under realistic clinical conditions.

The full study was published in the journal Optica.

#6379. Flowers with clear petal ‘windows’ carry fewer microbes, which influences pollinators

Clear petal windows let infrared heat into two Florida shrubs' blooms, and warmth, not ultraviolet, thins out the flower microbes inside.

Some flowers have tiny, clear windows built right into their petals. While they might just look like a pretty design, researchers at Florida Atlantic University (FAU) have discovered that these see-through spots actually control the temperature inside the flower, changing the nectar and affecting how insects pollinate them.

Ultraviolet is the part of sunlight known for killing microbes, so the windows looked like a way of letting the sun scrub a flower clean.

Instead, the heat-carrying infrared coming through them is what mattered: warmer flowers held fewer microbes, and the ultraviolet didn’t explain the difference.

Jessica Williams, a Ph.D. student at Florida Atlantic University, did the work with four colleagues. They focused on shrubs named Lyonia lucida (also called fetterbush), and Lyonia fruticosa.

They are close relatives in the heath family that also includes blueberries. Both grow in the sandy, sun-baked scrub of south-central Florida and bloom together in late spring.

Each flower is a narrow urn with its petals fused into a chamber, and near the base of that urn a patch of petal has almost no pigment in it.

Other members of the family have the same windows, blueberries among them, and Williams’ team asked what they do to the light and heat inside.

Fetterbush flowers are visited mostly by moths at night, while L. fruticosa gets bees and wasps. Those visitors are probably how most microbes reach a flower.

Over three days in May 2025 at Archbold Biological Station, the team took seven flowers from each of nine plants per species, 126 in all.

For every flower, a thin temperature probe went in through the opening to the base of the chamber while a second probe hung just outside the petals.

Then the flower was clipped off with sterile scissors, dropped into a tube and kept on ice. Within five hours it was rinsed with a few drops of sterile water, pumped in and out five times.

That rinse went onto growth plates for two days at 81°F (27°C), and the team counted the colonies of yeast, mold and bacteria that grew.

Across the 108 flowers with a full set of measurements, the warmer a flower was inside, the fewer microbes grew from its rinse. Yeasts were the most common, then molds, then bacteria, and in both species the warmer flowers had fewer yeasts.

The two shrubs didn’t respond the same way. In L. fruticosa, warmer flowers had fewer bacteria, while in fetterbush the temperature made little difference to the bacteria. Fetterbush also carried more mold.

A fetterbush flower warmed by a bit more than half a degree for every degree the air around it warmed. An L. fruticosa flower barely moved, staying warmer than the air when the air was cool and cooler than the air when it was hot.

So a microbe’s experience of a hot May day depends on which shrub it landed in.

Heat was already known to matter to these microbes. A 2022 study in Frontiers in Microbiology found that heat can change which bacteria live in a flower’s nectar.

The windows let through more light than the pigmented petal, both ultraviolet and infrared. So the team tested the obvious idea, that ultraviolet was sterilizing the flower.

A germicidal ultraviolet lamp did kill. After 30 seconds under it, the share of L. fruticosa rinses with any yeast fell from 90 to 60 percent.

But microbes from flowers whose windows let through more ultraviolet were no better at surviving the lamp than microbes from flowers that let through less. The lamp was probably harsher than the ultraviolet a flower typically sees inside, Williams’ team wrote.

Infrared was a different story. In May 2026 the team chilled cut flowers in a refrigerator, then set them under a 500-watt halogen work light behind a filter.

One filter passed only deep red and infrared, and the other blocked infrared and passed only visible light. A probe inside each flower logged its temperature for 10 minutes.

Fetterbush flowers under infrared alone warmed about 5.8°F (3.21°C) more than flowers with the infrared blocked. After 10 minutes, they were 12.9°F (7.18°C) above where they started.

L. fruticosa flowers warmed about the same amount under either filter. Infrared, in other words, does warm a fetterbush flower.

Williams’ team doesn’t claim the windows evolved to keep microbes out. The chain they describe runs the other way. The windows let infrared in and, in fetterbush at least, the infrared warms the flower.

The warmth then probably makes the flower a harder place for microbes to persist. Microbes were still present in warm flowers, only fewer of them.

The windows may be doing several other jobs at once, the team wrote. Those could run from helping pollen develop to changing how bright the inside of the flower looks to a visiting insect. Fewer microbes would then be a side effect of those jobs.

“One of the exciting things about this work is that a seemingly small floral trait can change the physical environment inside a flower in ways that affect its microbial community,” Williams said.

“Because floral microbes can influence nectar traits and plant-pollinator interactions, these results suggest that flower structure may have ecological consequences that extend beyond the flower itself.”

Nectar and pollinators were not measured here. The field sampling covered 18 plants at one station over three days, and growth plates count only the microbes that will grow in a lab dish.

The team measured heat, not who delivered the microbes. Moths and bees bring different passengers, and which ones arrive first and how they compete inside the flower also shape which microbes settle in.

How those arrivals interact with the heat is, in the team’s words, an open question.

A warmer flower may also keep a different set of microbes rather than simply fewer, a subset that can take the heat. The study didn’t test that.

Finding out would mean identifying which microbes each kind of visitor drops off and which of them survive a warm afternoon inside a fetterbush flower.

The full study was published in the journal New Phytologist.

A new study supports a more nuanced approach to obesity diagnosis. Here's what to know.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Obesity is linked to a range of health problems ‪—‬ including heart disease, diabetes and early death ‪—‬ but it can be hard to know who is most at risk for these outcomes. Doctors and researchers often use body mass index (BMI) as a convenient tool to assess patients, but this metric does not account for individual differences in body composition, scientists have long argued.

"BMI misses a lot of information," Dr. Francesco Rubino, a professor of bariatric and metabolic surgery at King's College London, told Live Science.

Rubino recently chaired a team of 56 experts that was assembled to better define obesity and develop new diagnostic criteria for the condition. First proposed in January 2025, their new framework includes more body measurements beyond BMI and distinguishes between "preclinical" and "clinical" obesity.

Now, a new study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature confirms that these new criteria could detect obesity with greater precision than BMI alone. In other words, with the new approach, more people would be accurately diagnosed with obesity and fewer people would be misdiagnosed than are with BMI alone.

Live Science spoke with Rubino and other experts to break down the new findings and learn what they mean for patients.

At the simplest level, obesity is excess body fat. There are special scans and exams that send weak electrical signals through the body to measure a person's body fat percentage directly, but criteria based on body measurements are more accessible across clinical settings.

BMI is the most common of these measurements, as it simply involves dividing a person's weight by their height squared. However, it does not account for individual differences in lean muscle mass or bone density.

BMI doesn't capture nuances and variation between patients, experts argue, and it limits what doctors can say about a given person's health risk.

Additionally, the different BMI categories — such as "overweight" and "obese" — don't carry the same risks for all patients. Certain racial and ethnic groups tend to experience health consequences, such as higher mortality rates, at different BMI levels than others do.

For a given patient being assessed for obesity, the proposed guidelines would suggest using at least one additional body measurement alongside BMI and having their doctor review their medical history for other signs of bodily or organ dysfunction.

The proposed body measurements are less influenced by a person's muscle mass or bone structure than BMI is. They include waist circumference, waist-to-hip ratio and waist-to-height ratio. Notably, because different ethnicities are associated with different fat distribution patterns in the body, the latest Nature study incorporated different waist circumference cutoffs based that varied by ethnicity.

In addition to these body measurements, the proposed criteria look at 18 conditions and signs of bodily or organ dysfunction that are related to obesity, such as cardiovascular diseases, joint pain and sleep apnea. (All 18 factors can be found detailed in this chart.)

Rubino and his colleagues — which together made up what's known as a Lancet Commission — defined "clinical obesity" as a disease state involving at least one of 18 forms of bodily dysfunction caused by excess fat tissue. Preclinical obesity, by contrast, is when a person is at risk of this disease state and may need interventions to avoid obesity-related dysfunction.

That means that two people with the same BMI, waist circumference and waist-to-height ratio may be classified differently, depending on whether they have other conditions. In the new study, between 77% and 91% of individuals with preclinical obesity did not progress to clinical obesity within 10 years, depending on the cohort analyzed.

This distinction can be complicated, though, as the diagnostic metrics for each form of dysfunction contain their own ambiguities.

"There needs to be more consensus on what's actually defining clinical obesity," said Dr. Aayush Visaria, an internal medicine instructor at Rutgers Robert Wood Johnson Medical School in New Jersey. Visaira was not involved in writing the new criteria but authored an analysis of the proposed measures.

The Lancet Commission argues that the categories of preclinical and clinical obesity could help doctors identify the people with the greatest need for treatment. The researchers tracked health outcomes using electronic health records from China, the United Kingdom, the United States and Spain, and they determined that their clinical obesity classification was better at flagging people's risk of death than BMI alone.

Changing the diagnostic criteria for obesity could, in turn, change who is recommended to receive weight-control medications.

They found no clear association between BMI and mortality risk, but clinical obesity was linked to a 69% greater risk of all-cause mortality, compared to no obesity.

The Lancet Commission's approach could drive a small net uptick in individuals diagnosed with obesity, according to the new study.

Under the current framework, "we are definitely missing some people who actually need obesity treatment but just did not meet the BMI criteria," said Dr. Jennifer Hwang, an instructor of medicine at the University of Chicago who has published her own analysis of the new criteria.

With the BMI-only approach, people with BMIs of 30 or higher are categorized as obese. With the new definition, some people with BMIs under 30 would be newly categorized as clinically obese, while a smaller group of people with high BMIs would suddenly not count as clinically obese, the Nature study predicted.

For instance, the former group might include people who have "overweight" BMIs but also have obesity-related dysfunction, while the latter group might include people with "obese" BMIs but without any dysfunction.

Overall, the new criteria would increase obesity prevalence by about 3.3% to 7.4%, the team predicted. The percentage varied depending on the group analyzed.

More research is needed to prove that the Lancet Commission's criteria would improve patient care and be practical to use in a clinical setting, Hwang said. She noted potential challenges in implementing both new aspects of the new framework. While the body measurements sound simple enough to use, clinicians would need training to perform them accurately.

Providers also may struggle with the new distinction between preclinical and clinical obesity. A 2025 analysis of the Lancet Commission framework noted that some patients who qualify for obesity medications under the Food and Drug Administration's guidelines may be recharacterized as having preclinical obesity and no longer receive a prescription.

Rubino and the rest of the Lancet Commission plan to continue validating their framework to see how it could best support personalized obesity treatment. For instance, they want to determine which forms of organ dysfunction are of greatest concern and develop a way of scoring each patient's level of risk.

Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts. Nature, 659. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5

#6375. Fossil fuel emissions are down in 2026. Green energy isn’t the reason

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The decrease is probably temporary and a result of high gas prices from the Iran war

The disruption of oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Iran has raised oil and gas prices around the world. According to new projections, those higher fuel prices will decrease global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuel burning in 2026 by about 0.16 gigatons from 2025.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Scientists project that global carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels will decrease by 0.4 percent this year, after having grown by 0.8 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025.

But the dip may not last. The lower emissions are probably driven by high oil prices stemming from the Iran war, researchers report November 9 in Nature Climate Change.

Global emissions probably would have grown again this year without the energy shock of the Iran war, says Glen Peters, a climate scientist at the Center for International Climate Research in Oslo, Norway. “So the energy transition that’s happening … it’s not quite big enough to get emissions heading downward yet.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

For the study, Peters and his colleagues used data on countries’ electric vehicle stocks and wind and solar energy generation to project those technologies impacts on global fossil CO2 emissions through 2028. The team used the generative AI model Claude to source data and write code for analysis.

By year’s end, global emissions will reach 38.24 gigatons, the researchers found, which is about 0.16 gigatons less than were emitted in 2025. For comparison, annual global emissions fell by nearly two gigatons in 2020 due to the COVID-19 pandemic and by about 0.5 gigatons in 2009 because of the global financial crisis.

If electric vehicle sales and solar and wind capacity continue growing at the rates they did in 2026, those technologies should counteract about 63 percent of the growth in emissions from 2025 to 2028 — or help avoid about 1.64 gigatons of added emissions.

The results indicate that the energy transition needs to accelerate if humankind is to realize consistently declining emissions, though EVs, solar and wind are already having a large impact. Without the offset in emissions provided by those technologies, global emissions would have risen by 1.9 percent each year on average from 2019 to 2025, the researchers note.

It’s very hard to say exactly how long it will take for humanity to reach peak emissions, Peters says. However, he notes, “the fact that we’re talking about this means that we’re close to that point.”

Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica, contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A tiny brown mushroom found in Florida's swamps is the first known fungus to contain both psilocybin, the chemical compound in psychedelic mushrooms; and amatoxin, the poisonous substance in the world's deadliest mushrooms.

The species, Galerina indica, has been nicknamed the "dark magic mushroom" and was characterized in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Current Biology.

"There is no species of mushroom anywhere, in any group, that has been known to produce both at the same time," study first author Andrew Kunik, a fungal biology researcher at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "So it's quite remarkable."

Exactly why the dark magic mushroom has evolved to contain these two compounds is unclear, but the authors told Live Science that they may give the fungus a powerful defense against being eaten.

The ability to produce either psychedelic or toxic chemicals has evolved multiple times across fungal lineages. A process called horizontal gene transfer, which is widespread among fungi, has played a part in that process.

In horizontal gene transfer an organism passes new genetic material to another, as opposed to vertical gene transfer, in which a parent passes genetic material to offspring. It can lead to unexpected genetic combinations and, in bacteria, plays a key role in the development of antibiotic resistance.

The tiny mushrooms seem to have acquired both psychedelic and toxic compounds via horizontal gene transfer.

Some of the world's deadliest mushrooms, from the Amanita genus, stop cells from producing proteins and can cause death through liver failure. Past work has shown these mushrooms shared the ability to produce their poisonous amatoxins via horizontal gene transfer with mushrooms from the unrelated genera Galerina and Lepiota. Some mushrooms have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer as well.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But Kunik and colleagues weren't looking for specific chemicals when they began hunting for Galerina mushrooms in the swamps of Florida; they just wanted to learn more about the mushrooms' chemical makeup, as not all Florida Galerina mushrooms had been characterized before.

To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that.

They collected five specimens from Galerina, a genus that contains over 300 species worldwide, many of which are poisonous. Among the samples they collected were small G. indica specimens that grew on moss-covered palm trunks. The largest mushrooms were only about 0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) tall, with caps up to about 0.1 inches (0.25 cm) wide.

Chemical analyses revealed that the dark magic mushroom contained both psilocybin and amatoxins, including one amatoxin that had never been documented in mushrooms. The new amatoxin wasn't wholly unexpected, given that other species of Galerina produce closely related amatoxins, Kunik said.

The production of psilocybin alongside the amatoxins was more of a surprise for the research team.

"To find them both together in one mushroom, I never expected to find that," study co-author Matthew E. Smith, a plant pathologist at the University of Florida, told Live Science. "We were shocked."

To understand how the tiny, deadly mushroom acquired its mind-altering, liver-poisoning abilities, the team compared the genes of G. indica with those of other psilocybin-producing mushrooms, finding the genes shared a common evolutionary origin — even though the mushrooms themselves are distantly related.

Scanning electron microscopy image of the spores from the “dark magic mushroom”.

The researchers also found G. indica’s psilocybin-producing genes are arranged in a different order than in other psilocybin-producing fungi, which suggests the gene cluster was rearranged during its evolutionary history, a clue that horizontal gene transfer happened.

G. indica seems to have acquired the ability to produce psilocybin via horizontal gene transfer from unrelated fungi about 15.5 million years ago, based on reconstructions of Galerina’s evolutionary history from DNA analysis, Smith said. However, it’s possible that psilocybin-producing genes entered the lineage through two separate horizontal gene transfer events, possibly as recently as 6 million years ago, Kunik noted. Collecting and sequencing more Galerina specimens could help untangle their evolutionary history.

The findings are surprising, said Hannah Reynolds, a fungal ecologist at Western Connecticut State University who was not involved with the new research. "What was exciting about this paper was seeing both of these [compounds] present, seeing that this gene cluster jumped in, got rearranged, maybe came in twice — it's very cool," Reynolds told Live Science.

The ability to produce two types of incapacitating chemicals could form a powerful defense against being eaten, because organisms that would normally eat them would have difficulty evolving defenses against both, Kunik speculated.

But the idea that this duo of compounds prevents the mushroom from being eaten is just a hypothesis. To buttress that idea, further research might tweak the genes of the dark magic mushroom to observe how removing one compound affects the species' role in the food web, Kunik suggested.

Tropical and subtropical mushrooms are historically understudied, so there is likely much more incredible fungal diversity right under our feet, Smith said.

Kunik et al. (2026). "The 'dark magic mushroom' co-produces amatoxins and psilocybin." Current Biology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2026.10.041

#6372. Toxic secrets are hiding in Arctic ice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A century-old pollution trail leads scientists back to Montana mining

At the turn of the twentieth century, the Anaconda Smelter in Montana spewed arsenic into the air — those heavy metal particles that are now trapped in Arctic ice cores.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ice cores record Earth’s secrets, even the dirty ones.

Some of the cylindrical sections of ice extracted from the Arctic contain elevated levels of arsenic, lead and other heavy metals that circulated in our planet’s atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Those pollutants, which have been tied to declines in IQ and higher rates of certain cancers, were probably emitted by a mining and smelting company in Montana whose grounds are now designated as multiple Superfund sites, the researchers report November 3 in Nature Sustainability.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ice cores contain tiny particles that were once airborne — including pollutants, volcanic ash and salt from ocean spray — and fell to our planet’s surface within a few days or weeks. In polar regions, that fallout combines with snow and is preserved as ice.

Joseph McConnell, an environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, and his collaborators recently analyzed 10 ice cores collected across Canada, Greenland and Russia. The cores contained material that had fallen to Earth as early as 210 BCE, but the interval spanning the Industrial Revolution in the United States — from roughly 1870 to 1914 — was what caught the team’s collective eye.

In the ice layers from that period, arsenic concentrations in some of the ice cores were up to 15 times higher than pre-Industrial Revolution levels. Because the heavy metal exposure has been tied to upticks in the rates of certain cancers, McConnell and his team set out to determine the most likely source of all that pollution.

The largest increases in arsenic existed in the ice cores from Greenland. That finding was a big hint, McConnell says, because atmospheric circulation patterns tend to move material from west to east. “The only way you can explain that pattern of deposition is if the emissions are coming from North America,” McConnell says. “Had it been from Europe, we would have seen much larger increases in the Russian Arctic.”

The most likely source, the team concluded, was a massive copper mining and smelting operation in southwestern Montana operated by the Anaconda Copper Mining Company. It was one of the largest in North America during the Industrial Revolution and, unlike other copper mining operations in the area, it worked with copper ore that contained heavy metals like arsenic and lead. It was no secret that those toxic metals were entering the atmosphere, says Fred Quivik, a historian and the author of Smoke and Tailings, a book about the environmental history of copper smelting in Montana. “Ranchers and farmers started seeing their livestock die from arsenic poisoning.”

Based on the concentrations of arsenic in the ice cores and models of how material disperses in the atmosphere, McConnell and his colleagues estimated that the Anaconda Copper Mining Company was emitting roughly 30 tons of arsenic per day into the atmosphere in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. By comparison, Chile, currently the world’s largest producer of copper and home to more than 20 mining operations, collectively emits roughly one quarter as much arsenic today.

Beginning in 1919, the Anaconda Copper Mining Company installed devices near its smokestacks and other facilities to capture arsenic and prevent its release into the atmosphere. Arsenic emissions dropped by about 60 percent as a result, the ice core data showed, but by then hundreds of thousands of nearby residents had already been exposed for decades. That exposure could have been lessened, McConnell says, if the Anaconda Copper Mining Company hadn’t waited so long to install the pollution-abatement technology. “They delayed installation for about a decade.”

These new findings should be combined with census records to trace the effects of this pollution on human health in the 19th and 20th centuries, McConnell and his team suggest. “We hope that epidemiologists will take this information and really investigate potential impacts on human populations.”

A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have proposed a new tabletop device to detect the subtle way Earth's daily spin on its axis twists the space-time around it ‪—‬ an effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

If built, the sensor could measure the quantum effect known as frame dragging with the same precision as the best satellite experiments, but in minutes instead of years, the researchers proposed in a new study.

The research, published Sept. 17 in the journal Physical Review Letters, aimed to address a classic mismatch in physics. Picture a ring of clocks bolted to a spinning merry-go-round. You synchronize each clock with its neighbor around the ring. Then, you compare the last clock with the first. They don't match.

"It is impossible to synchronize that collection of clocks when you're in a rotating frame," Kai-Isaak Ellers, a physics graduate student at the University of California, Berkeley (UC Berkeley) and first author of the study, told Live Science.

A photo of scientists working on NASA's Gravity Probe B in 2003. This device measured Earth's frame-dragging from space, confirming Einstein's predictions with an 18% margin of error.

Einstein's theory of general relativity predicts that a massive, spinning object drags the fabric of space-time along with it, just like a spoon twirling in honey. The effect is clearly visible around supermassive objects, like the Milky Way's central black hole. But around Earth, the effect is very faint.

So far, scientists have measured Earth's frame dragging only from orbit. They tracked how the twisting of space-time slowly shifts spinning gyroscopes or the paths of satellites. In 2011, NASA's Gravity Probe B satellite, which carried four gyroscopes, confirmed Einstein's prediction with a margin of error of about 18%. Satellites tracked with lasers have since done even better. In July, researchers reported in the journal Nature that the LARES-2 satellite had shrunk that margin of error to just 0.2%.

However, that took about three years of laser tracking. Researchers also had to account for the fact that Earth bulges at the equator and its mass is spread unevenly, which gives the planet’s gravity small irregularities that tug on satellites far more strongly than frame dragging does. To subtract those tugs, the team relied on detailed maps of Earth's gravity made by other satellites.

Measuring frame dragging more precisely is a way to stress-test general relativity. Several alternative theories of gravity predict a slightly different amount of twisting, and a lab-based measurement would also be free of the modeling assumptions that satellite experiments depend on, Ellers said.

The new device is a loop of superfluid helium-4 — helium chilled until it flows without friction and behaves like a single, giant quantum object. The loop is interrupted by a thin barrier riddled with tiny holes, called a Josephson junction. Superfluid helium can slip through the holes, but ordinary liquid helium cannot.

"That's where the quantum behavior comes from," said K. Birgitta Whaley, a quantum physicist at UC Berkeley and a co-author of the study.

As Earth spins and drags space-time, it nudges the quantum state of the helium flowing through the junction. That nudge shifts the frequency at which the helium sloshes back and forth in the loop, which the researchers could detect.

A visualization of Earth's uneven gravity field taken by NASA's Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment in 2009. The lumpiness of our planet's gravitational field makes it harder to precisely measure relativistic effects.

Superfluid devices, many of them built at UC Berkeley, have detected Earth's rotation since the late 1990s. But the helium-4 versions built around a Josephson junction, like the new design, have worked within about a hundredth of a degree of 2.17 K (minus 455.76 Fahrenheit, or minus 270.98 Celsius), the temperature at which helium-4 becomes a superfluid. At that temperature, a lingering fraction of "normal" helium mixed in with the superfluid adds noise.

Instead, the team calculated how the device would behave at a few thousandths of a degree above absolute zero. Below 0.7 K, the noise changed character, and the team found it drops sharply as the helium gets colder. One key finding in the new paper is the result of the team's thermal noise analysis, which showed how sensitive these devices could be at millikelvin temperatures, Elles said.

The catch is the barrier. Earlier helium-4 devices used holes about 90 nanometers wide. Working at these frigid temperatures demands much smaller holes, about 1 nanometer across ‪—‬ roughly the size of a helium atom. Keith Schwab, a physicist at Caltech and co-author of the study, and his collaborators are developing such materials, but they haven't been built into a working sensor yet.

If they can be, the researchers calculate that the device could measure frame dragging to 0.2% precision in about 35 minutes. If its vibrating membrane were made from the lowest-loss crystals, such as quartz or sapphire, that could drop to about one second, they said.

"This seems to be a very serendipitous discovery that at millikelvin, we can get this high sensitivity," Whaley told Live Science.

The signal corresponds to a time difference of about 10-35 seconds between helium flowing one way around the loop and the other — the same mismatch as the clocks on the metaphorical merry-go-round.

"The interesting thing about it is just how small it is," Whaley said. "It's not so far off from the Planck time," about 10-44 seconds, the shortest slice of time before the known laws of physics are expected to break down. This experiment is still a billion times too large to reach that limit, Whaley said. But future helium experiments could help explore whether time flows smoothly, like a ramp, or ticks forward in tiny, indivisible jumps, like the frames of a movie.

Ellers, K.-I., Christodoulou, M., Schwab, K. C., & Whaley, K. B. (2026). Quantum sensing of gravitational frame dragging with a superfluid ⁴He gyrometer. Physical Review Letters, 137(12), 121404. https://doi.org/10.1103/q3v9-rjm9

Larissa G. Capella is a science writer based in Washington state. She obtained a B.S. in physics and a B.A. in English creative writing in 2024, which enabled her to pursue a career that integrates both disciplines. She reports mainly on environmental, Earth and physical sciences, but is always willing to write about any science that sparks her curiosity. Her work has appeared in Eos, Science News, Space.com, among others.
