#6294. Faye Travel Insurance: The Best New Company Out there

We may receive compensation from Faye as an advertising partner. However, this does not influence our evaluations. Our opinions are our own.

I’ve been writing about travel for nearly two decades and, in that time, I’ve watched the travel insurance industry change at roughly the speed of a glacier. For years, the pitch was always the same: buy a policy, hope you never need it, and if something goes wrong, prepare for a paperwork marathon and a check that arrives somewhere between “eventually” and “you’ve forgotten you ever filed.”

I’ve personally been on the receiving end of that runaround. So have most travelers I know. It’s just something you kind of deal with. After all, you should never, ever, ever, EVER travel without travel insurance. You don’t want to end up needing a GoFundMe to pay your bills and get home if something goes wrong. (You can’t predict the future!)

Now, there’s a lot of players in this space but one I want to highlight today is Faye Travel Insurance, which I think is doing something unique.

Faye is a digital-first travel insurance company that launched coverage in the U.S. in 2022 so it’s pretty new to the US market when you consider that brands like World Nomads or Allianz have been offering coverage for over twenty years.

Faye is based on a pretty simple idea: travel insurance shouldn’t just sit there waiting for things to go wrong. It should actively help things go right.

That means whole-trip protection (your trip, your health, your stuff, even your pet), an app that’s actually useful while you’re traveling, 24/7 access to real human customer support, claims that get processed in days instead of months, and a digital wallet that pays you back almost instantly instead of waiting around for a check in the mail, which some companies still do in this day and age.

Faye has one plan for domestic and international trips, which makes things super easy. A lot of travel insurance companies have lots of plans and you end up squinting at coverage tables trying to figure out which one isn’t going to leave you stranded and has the coverage minimums you need. Faye built a single comprehensive plan that covers most of what travelers actually need:

These limits are pretty standard, especially on the medical coverage. If you want to add stuff on, they have a few optional addons that I think are really good and unique:

The CFAR insurance is really useful and I’ve rarely seen a company allow you to add it on to a policy. Usually, it’s already incorporated at a higher fee but this creates an affordable add on. I also love the pet care add on as more and more people travel with their pets.

Here’s where Faye really separates itself. Faye built something completely different! Here’s what you can actually do inside the Faye app:

Buy a policy in as little as 60 seconds – Plug in your trip details, get a quote, get covered.

Get real-time flight tracking and alerts – You’ll get delay info, gate changes, or baggage carousel numbers when you land! A lot of apps do this but this is a nice add on.

Telemedicine – Faye gives you access to a network of 20,000 telemedicine doctors in 21 languages when you travel abroad. If you wake up with food poisoning in a town where you don’t speak the language and don’t trust the local hospital reviews, you can talk to a doctor from your hotel bed. (As someone who has had to find doctors in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Find a doctor, pharmacy, ER, or ATM nearby – The app does the work of figuring out where to go when you’re disoriented and just need to find the closest open pharmacy at 11 p.m. in a city you arrived in five hours ago. (As someone who has had to do this in other countries, this feature is amazing!)

Get free airport lounge access – If your flight is delayed by three hours or more, Faye gets you into a lounge – and who wouldn’t want lounge access with free food and drinks for a long delay?

Store your documents in Safekeeping – Securely u     pload your passport, visa, insurance card, vaccination records. If anything gets lost or stolen, you’ve got digital copies.

Check destination essentials before you go – Visa requirements, plug adapter types, local emergency numbers, weather, currency conversion, even local apps worth downloading.

Chat with real humans, 24/7 – Actual customer experience specialists, available every day of the year, including weekends and holidays.

Buy an eSIM – The app also enables you to purchase an eSIM meaning you can avoid pesky physical SIM swaps and get connected to the internet right when you land.

Here’s how Faye works: something bad happens. You open the app. You file a claim in a few minutes by uploading photos of your receipts. If it’s a qualifying issue like a baggage delay or flight delay, you may get reimbursed almost instantly. Funds go straight into Faye Wallet, a digital payment card built into the app that connects to Apple Pay or Google Pay. You tap and pay, right then and there, for whatever you actually need: a new outfit, toiletries, dinner, a hotel.

For larger or more complex claims, Faye aims to resolve them within 48 hours. of receiving the necessary documentation.

If you don’t want to use the digital wallet, you can transfer the funds to your bank account or get a paper check.

Pricing depends on your trip cost, destination, length, state of residence and age (same as every insurance product) but prices start at around $5.16 a day for international trips, which is a lot more competitive than other companies out there.

I’ve used a lot of travel insurance companies over the years. Most of them are fine. A few are awful. Faye is the first one that feels like it was designed by people who actually understand modern travel and get that we’re booking trips on our phones, communicating in apps, and expecting the same digital convenience from insurance that we get from everything else.

The combination of whole-trip protection, the app, Faye Wallet, real human support, and fast claims has genuinely changed how I think about this category. Travel insurance used to be the thing I bought and forgot.

If you’re heading out on a trip soon, check it out at withfaye.com, get a quote, and see for yourself.

#6293. Nomad Citizen: A New Social Safety Net for Entrepreneurs

If you’re a digital nomad or a location-independent business owner, you’re either overpaying for fragmented insurance coverage (travel, medical, etc.) or just badly underinsured. You have a health plan, travel insurance, and maybe some medical evacuation coverage. But, when you work for yourself, you lack the kind of safety net protections you get with a corporate job. And you cannot use a country’s social safety net because, well, you’re not a citizen, right? You’re just roaming the world!

The travel insurance company Safety Wing is looking to change that. They have always wanted to create this all-in-one package for digital nomads that includes insurance, employee benefits, and a social safety net.

I use their travel insurance all the time and they have just launched what they call Nomad Citizen that seeks to address the gaps in coverage.

Nomad Citizen is an annual membership that bundles health coverage, travel protection, income protection, and life insurance benefits into a single plan. It’s for location-independent entrepreneurs and business owners who spend more than half the year outside their home country and whose lives and income cross borders as a default.

Nomad Citizen covers you globally with no residency restrictions (except for Puerto Rico).

Nomad Citizen covers people under 56 and earning at least $4,000 USD per month. You sign up online, choose your start date, declare that you’re in good health, and confirm you’ll be outside your passport country for more than half the year. You can also add your partner and any children under 18.

But who should sign-up? This is an interesting product. I definitely think there’s a niche for it. After all, let’s say you’re an entrepreneur in Bali and don’t have access to any social safety net. What happens if you get sick or really hurt and you’re out of work? A friend of mine in Mexico was hit by a car and severely hospitalized and ate into his travel insurance limits really quickly. Afterwards, he couldn’t work for months while he was in rehab and started a GoFundMe for help. A product like Nomadic Citizen would have helped him. Or helped any of the other digital nomads who get injured on the road and have to raise funds.

I think this product is good for someone who is living in a country outside their own without access to social services and a robust social safety net. For example, if you live in Sweden and have access to all the benefits of the State, this product probably isn’t for you because they have tons of services but if you live in Thailand, Mexico, Indonesia, or France but don’t have access to benefits, or are just roaming the world, have a high income, work on your own, or have a family, then this product would be something to consider.

For those signing up on or after July 1, 2026, the Nomad Citizen membership costs $443 per month for those 18 to 39. If you’re 40 – 49, it’s $665 per month, and $875 per month for 50-55. Children cost $143 per month (couples on the plan can add their first child under 10 at no cost). You can pay monthly or annually.

A note about US coverage: Nomad Citizen is truly worldwide, including the US, although it should be noted that coverage limits were not designed for extensive use there…because well, the US health care system is just a mess.

Income protection: The income protection benefit is probably the single most compelling reason Nomad Citizen exists. Traditional income protection or disability insurance requires a fixed employer, a permanent address, and residency in a specific country. Freelancers and sole traders working across borders are essentially uninsurable for income loss through conventional schemes, such as government assistance.

If you’re a freelancer or remote worker and you lose your income (you’re laid off, your contracts dry up, or you can’t work due to a medical condition), Nomad Citizen pays you up to $4,000 per month for up to 3 or 6 months while you get back on your feet. That benefit doesn’t exist anywhere else!

Health insurance: Up to $1.5 million in annual coverage for inpatient, outpatient, prescriptions, dental, vision, mental health, maternity, preventive care, wellness therapies, and more. This is just like health insurance where you live and covers everything you need. It is far more robust than regular travel insurance, which is only there for emergencies.

Travel coverage: Trip delays, cancellations, stolen electronics, lost luggage, evacuation, robbery, family visits during hospitalisation.

Parental leave: If you have a baby or become a legal guardian of a child, they pay US$4,000/month so you can take time off work without worrying about money. There is a waiting period of 3 years to access this benefit.

Long-term disability: If something really serious happens to you and you are permanently forced to stop working because, for instance,  you lose your eyesight, you’re diagnosed with cancer, you have a major stroke, or you can no longer do basic things like walk, dress yourself, or eat on your own, they pay you US$4,000/month up to age 75.

Visa assistance: Members can browse and apply for different governments’ versions of long-term visas designed for nomads (i.e. they can work on those visas) directly through our app interface without having to apply through the government websites. They handle all the direct communication with the government and quality check your application before submission to maximize the chances of approval.

Nomad Care Map: Find the best providers through their member-powered database of more than 4000 healthcare providers all over the world, with ratings for service and English level.

Payment cards: Use your SafetyWing card to pay for covered services up to $500. This auto-generates a claim that has already been paid so you do not have to wait for reimbursement. The SafetyWing card is a worldwide prepaid debit card that is sent to every Nomad Citizen member, which they can use to pay for doctor’s appointments or prescriptions without using their own money.

24/7 human support: You’ll have access to 24/7 live chat so you can get an answer from a real person within a few minutes.

Everything in one app: Claims, coverage details, customer care, provider search with Nomad Care Map, and visa assistance are all managed through a single app. There is no need to switch between a health insurer, a travel insurer, and a separate income protection provider (if one existed).

For health coverage, you either pay out of pocket and file for reimbursement or contact the 24/7 team to arrange direct payment with the provider. For travel claims, you collect documentation (police reports, carrier delay notices, receipts) and submit a claim. For income protection, you work with SafetyWing to verify the loss and provide evidence that you’re actively seeking new income. Everything is managed through one app and they make it really simple and easy to do.

I love SafetyWing’s mission and use their travel insurance on all my trips. This new Nomad Citizen product is perfect for people who are full-time digital nomads and want some sort of income protection as well as more robust health and travel coverage and the kind of social safety programs you would get if you lived in one place. After all, when you are a solopreneur, you do worry about what happens if you get injured, can’t work, or have a kid. It’s all on you, right? Nomad Citizen is the program that ensures that you won’t have to worry about this kind of stuff anymore.

Staying at Walt Disney World on hotel points — within walking distance of two theme parks — might sound like a pixie-dust-fueled dream, but it's actually possible if you stay at the Walt Disney World Swan, Dolphin or Swan Reserve.

These large, highly visible properties are actually three adjacent but distinct hotels that share access to amenities.

The Dolphin is the 27-story pyramid that opened in 1990 and is visible from just about every Disney World theme park.

The Swan opened in 1990 and is home to two 47-foot swan statues, while the Swan Reserve is the newest of the trio, having just opened in 2021.

These three resorts are clustered together and are all bookable with Marriott Bonvoy points. This is possible because while they each have Walt Disney World in their names and in their location, the Dolphin is actually a Sheraton, the Swan is a Westin and the Swan Reserve is in Marriott's Autograph Collection.

Related: These are the best credit cards for earning Marriott Bonvoy points

That means that the current welcome bonus with the (see rates and fees) that awards three free night awards (valued up to 50,000 Marriott points each; certain hotels have resort fees) after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first three months of account opening could cover a three-night stay at one of these properties. And that's especially true if you were willing to top up your awards with up to 25,000 additional Marriott points if the nights you wanted cost a few more points than 50,000. Additionally, new cardholders can receive up to $100 in statement credits (up to $50 biannually) after spending $500 on eligible airline purchases (through June 30, 2027).

Generally speaking, the Walt Disney World Dolphin is a large, busy convention hotel with the most on-site restaurants and amenities. The Walt Disney World Swan is comparatively smaller but still a very large, busy hotel that's closest to the Dolphin, with both connected by a covered walkway.

The Swan Reserve is the smallest, most upscale — and most expensive — of the three properties. But combined, these three properties are positively massive with 2,619 rooms, 23 restaurants and lounges, and a host of amenities and facilities.

Due to some wheeling and dealing in the 1980s, the Swan and Dolphin (and later, Swan Reserve) scored some of the best real estate at Walt Disney World.

These resorts are within walking distance of both Epcot and Disney's Hollywood Studios. Or there's a complimentary water taxi that can take you to either of those parks that leaves from the dock between the Dolphin and the Swan.

Only three of Disney's own operated resorts can claim this same feature: Disney's Yacht Club, Disney's Boardwalk and Disney's Beach Club.

All of those are deluxe Disney resorts that regularly start between $600 - $800 per night, where rooms at this trio of properties can start at half that price if you're paying with cash.

Related: How to save hundreds of dollars on a trip to Disney with the Disney Inspire Visa

There are multiple pools at the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve, with each property having at least one pool located directly on-site.

But the most expansive pools are situated closest to the Dolphin, including the grotto pool with waterfalls and a waterslide.

There is also a lap pool in case you want to get a water-based workout in. A great thing about the pools — and other amenities — is that it doesn't matter which of these three hotels you are staying at; you can use all the amenities at the other hotels, too.

But it's not just pools you can pick from; there is a very long list of amenities in case the Disney parks leave you with some downtime.

At the Dolphin, you'll find a good-sized arcade and even a small bowling alley.

Between the Swan and Dolphin, there is also sand volleyball, an outdoor playground area for little kids and even swan-themed paddle boats that guests can take out on the water at no additional cost, as rentals are included in the hefty $50 nightly resort fee.

If you wanted to have a resort day outside the theme parks during your Disney World vacation, the odds are high that there is plenty to do at the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve to keep you entertained.

Each of the three hotels also has its own fitness area for you to still get your workouts in.

If, after all that activity, you want to rest and enjoy a massage or another treatment, there is a Mandara Spa inside the Dolphin.

Believe it or not, the reason you can enjoy these Marriott hotels, located in the heart of Walt Disney World, dates back to disputes and deals in the 1980s.

The hotels have many Disney perks and an on-property Disney location, but they are not actually Disney-owned and operated hotels. And now they are all hotels where you can earn and use Marriott Bonvoy points to stay in the middle of Mickey's kingdom without paying Mickey's exact price tag.

Guests of the Walt Disney World Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve get to enjoy some really good Disney benefits that are otherwise mostly reserved only for true on-property Disney World guests.

As mentioned, there are complimentary boats to Epcot and Hollywood Studios from these hotels if you don't want to make the 15-20-minute walk.

There are buses that leave from these hotels to Magic Kingdom or Animal Kingdom. The one downside to the buses vs. those at "true" Disney resorts is that the bus to Magic Kingdom takes you to the Ticket and Transportation Center (TTC) instead of to Magic Kingdom itself. From the TTC, you have to take the monorail or ferry boat to the Magic Kingdom.

If that sounds like a hassle to you, it can be a good time to splurge on a Disney-operated Minnie Van you book in the Lyft app to take you directly to the front of the Magic Kingdom with the money you saved by staying at these hotels instead of actual deluxe Disney resorts.

At these hotels, you will find true Disney gift shops, along with Disney park tickets and Disney vacation planning assistance.

If by which hotel is best you mean the nicest, then the answer is likely the Walt Disney World Swan Reserve. It is not only the newest and most expensive of the three hotels, but also the one that falls under the higher-category Marriott Brand, Autograph Collection.

But everyone has different tastes and priorities for their Disney trip, so each of the three hotels has its own fans.

All three of the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve hotels are great choices for families, but if we have to choose, families with young kids may enjoy the Swan and Dolphin a bit more due to more on-site amenities such as the playground and arcade and a slightly shorter walk to the boats or to Epcot and Hollywood Studios.

There are also more on-site food options at the Dolphin and Swan than you'll find at the Swan Reserve.

In part because of conventions and events that do come to these hotels, no single hotel among the three is always the cheapest. The only real way to know for sure on your dates is to run some searches.

However, the Dolphin is the least expensive of the three on average, whether booking on Marriott points or cash, typically followed by the Swan and then the Swan Reserve.

All the rooms at these hotels are nice, especially once the Dolphin finishes its current renovation, but there are differences among them.

Swan Reserve rooms are likely the nicest between the three, with higher-end finishes, two robes available, walk-in showers, a better coffee maker, etc.

The rooms at the Swan are also nice and have been recently renovated. In my experience, they typically offer one robe, and importantly, two queen beds in the rooms with the two bed option.

The rooms at the Dolphin are currently undergoing renovation to make them more similar in appearance to the Swan. However, a significant difference will remain even after the renovations.

The beds at the Dolphin in rooms with two beds are full-sized or double beds, not queen beds. This makes it a tighter fit if you are putting two people in each bed.

There were no robes in our Dolphin room, and the coffee maker is a step down, which makes sense, as this is a Sheraton rather than the higher-tier brands at the other two hotels.

There are more restaurants at the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve than it makes sense for me to put in a big list here, but I will mention a few of my personal favorite options.

First, I'm a fan of Rosa Mexicano, especially for an easy, fun arrival-night dinner with margaritas — especially if I have a resort credit to put to good use, as I did recently by booking via Amex's Hotel Collection with my .

Amare, a Mediterranean restaurant at the Swan Reserve, and Todd English's bluezoo, a seafood restaurant in the Walt Disney World Dolphin, are two additional standouts for me, though there are plenty of other great picks, too.

And believe it or not, if you order an entrée at Todd English’s bluezoo, Amare, or Il Mulino New York Trattoria, Rosa Mexicano, Bourbon Steak or Kimonos, your kids ages 5 - 12 can get two free hours at the on-site Camp Dolphin. This supervised childcare includes a take-home craft and a snack.

I also enjoy the grab-and-go options that are available at each of these three hotels for an easy muffin and coffee sort of breakfast in the morning.

If you have Marriott Platinum elite status or higher — which you can get just by having the — you can choose free breakfast as your benefit for the stay, which will get you a daily voucher to use in these shops.

I've stayed at these hotels over a dozen times and there is no doubt in my mind that the Swan, Dolphin and Swan Reserve can absolutely be worth it when deciding between them and Disney-owned resorts.

And don't get me wrong — I really love a good, true Disney resort stay with all of the elaborate themes and locations — but the prices for deluxe resorts owned by Disney are often more than the prices that these three resorts charge. At these hotels, you're often paying a price that is more in the Disney moderate, mid-tier resort range (and sometimes even a value range), but getting closer to deluxe-tier location and amenities.

And you can even use some of your hotel credits from certain Amex or Chase cards and book via programs that give you free breakfast, resort credits and more, like I just did via American Express with my to get $450 in bonus savings and inclusions on a recent stay.

So there are ways you can really bring down your total cost here that typically don't work at true Disney resorts, which don't participate in most of those programs, including even using the simple $100 annual Chase Travel hotel credit from the (see rates and fees).

And that's assuming you're even paying cash — you can also use your Marriott points or free night awards here and save your cash for other parts of the trip.

So yes, I absolutely think it is sometimes worth potentially spending less to stay in the middle of it all at the Swan, Dolphin or Swan Reserve and still get the overwhelming majority of the perks of being at a true Disney resort.

There are a lot of great places to stay while on a Walt Disney World vacation, but often you have to make trade-offs. You can have a great location, good value, or an upscale stay, but typically not all three at the same time ... except at the Swan, Dolphin or Swan Reserve, which have the potential to give you the best of all worlds.

While the Swan Reserve is my favorite of the three, I've stayed at all of these hotels multiple times over the years on cash, Marriott points, and even using some of the hotel credits from my various credit cards, and I have every intention of many more stays in the future.

#6291. Holafly Plans: The Best eSIM Plan for Long Term Travelers

There are a lot of eSIM companies in the world. They all work a similar way: you download their app, pick your package, install the eSIM into your smartphone, and off you go. There’s many I like.

But one I like more than the rest is Holafly and I’ve been using their eSIMs for years. I find their app to be easy to use and their rates really competitive.

So when Holafly launched Holafly Plans, a single eSIM that works as an ongoing subscription across 160+ destinations, I was excited. It’s a great option for those who are looking for more data and flexibility than a traditional eSIM. (An eSIM is a digital SIM built directly into your phone’s hardware, so there’s no physical card to insert or swap. Instead of visiting a shop for a plastic SIM, you activate a plan by scanning a QR code or installing it through an app, and you’re connected within minutes. Because it’s software-based, a single phone can hold multiple eSIMs, letting you switch between a home number and a local or global travel plan without touching your device. I have like 10 installed. lol)

In this post, I’m going to explain what the product is, how it’s different than a traditional eSIM, and who I think this option is for!

Holafly Plans is a single global eSIM that covers more than 160 destinations on one ongoing subscription. You buy it once, install it once, and it just keeps working as you move from country to country. You don’t reswap SIMs, you don’t redownload anything, there’s no re-purchasing, and no hunting for a new QR code every time you land somewhere new.

It automatically reconnects you when you land in a new place. Think of it as like a traditional mobile carrier – but a lot cheaper.

You can buy it monthly or annually and it comes in two tiers: Light and Unlimited. There’s no annual contract and you can cancel any time.

The Unlimited Plan includes no data caps and an unlimited hotspot so you can tether your laptop on the go. If you’re a digital nomad uploading video, doing video calls, or just someone who doesn’t want to think about data ever again, this is a great add-on. This tier also comes with a local phone number from the US, UK, or Canada, which lets you receive SMS messages.

The Light Plan gives you 25GB of data a month, still includes a hotspot, and still covers the same 160+ destination coverage. For someone who mostly uses maps, messaging apps, and the occasional Instagram scroll, this package is probably the best option.

Additionally, with both Holafly Plans, once your plan is active, you get their “Always On” feature which is 1GB of backup data every month, automatically for life, even if you eventually cancel your subscription entirely.

Pricing varies a bit by region and currency and depending on how long you purchase, so check out their current rates on the Holafly Plans page. However, as an example, their unlimited plan is only $55 USD per month for 1 year, which is a lot cheaper than any US based carrier charges for their base option that includes unlimited 5G data overseas.  You can get monthly, quarterly, or yearly plans. Quarterly plans save approximately 10% while yearly plans save 15%.

Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

Classic Holafly eSIMs are built for a single trip. You pick a country or region (there are 200+ available), choose how many days of data you need, and it covers just that trip. If you’re flying to Portugal for two weeks, a classic eSIM is still the simpler, cheaper option. It’s a one-and-done purchase. If you only take a couple trips per year then this is still the best option.

On the other hand, if you’re a digital nomad who is gone from your home country most of the year and moving between different countries all the time, then the Holafly Plans fly is the much better option. It’s a standing global subscription designed for people who are more or less always somewhere. Instead of buying a new eSIM every time your itinerary changes, you have one number, one connection, one bill that follows you across borders indefinitely. Plus, you can get a phone number, unlimited data, and a hotspot. In the US, if you were to get T-Mobile’s plan, which caps data and is the closest thing we have to “affordable” international plans, you’re going to spend over $100 USD a month (I know because I used to use this plan!). Holafly Plans costs less and gives you more.

Holafly also recently launched a new tier called The Ultra Plan by Holafly, and it’s a bit different from anything else in the eSIM world.

Basically, it takes everything in the Unlimited Plan (unlimited data, hotspot, phone number, 160+ destinations) and adds a a small travel insurance component that ib:

How much does it cost? Ultra is $90.95 a month if you pay monthly, $82.65 a month on the quarterly plan, or $73.41 a month if you pay yearly. For comparison, Unlimited is $64.90 monthly, $58.65 quarterly, or $52.41 yearly. Quarterly saves you about 10%, and yearly about 20%. (Use my code NOMADICMATT or MATTK gets you another 10% off on top of whichever plan you choose.)

So, is the upgrade worth it? Ultra costs about $26 a month more than Unlimited if you pay monthly, $24 more on quarterly, and $21 more on yearly. Here’s how I think about it: one lost bag gets you $150, which covers roughly six months of the difference, whichever way you pay. A single doctor visit abroad, or one session with a psychologist, nutritionist, or personal trainer, can easily cost more than that. And that’s before you even factor in the language barrier and the stress of figuring out where to go. With Ultra, you get unlimited access to all that support included in your plan.

If you’re heading out for a few months, quarterly is the sweet spot. You get the savings without committing to a full year. If you’re taking a two-week vacation, skip it and stick with a standard Holafly eSIM.

Just to be clear, this doesn’t replace travel insurance. It won’t cover hospital bills, theft, or emergency situations, so you’ll still need proper travel insurance for all of that but if you want small trip related coverage, this can be a cheaper option.

Getting set up takes a couple of minutes, not a couple of hours:

If anything goes sideways during setup, real people are on the other end of support 24/7.

Holafly Plans isn’t for everyone. If you’re taking a single two-week vacation, a classic destination eSIM will cost you less. However, if you’re a frequent traveler who is in and out of multiple countries within a given month or a digital nomad who needs reliable, ongoing connectivity for work, not just casual browsing, then get Holafly Plans. It’s easier and will save you money in the long run.

****Holafly plans make life easier if you’re a long-term traveler. You don’t have to swap SIM cards, you get unlimited data, and you get a phone number. It’s the closest thing to a traditional phone plan that is out there but without any huge costs or data caps.

And, as someone who roams the world a lot and uses a lot of data, especially to stream video and use my phone as a hotspot, these plans save me a ton of money!

If you’re roaming the world and plan to be out of your home country for a while, this is the product to get!

Use the promo code NOMADICMATT at checkout to get 10% OFF Holafly Plans and 5% OFF all standard Holafly eSIMs.

Is Holafly Plans different from a regular Holafly eSIM? Yes. Regular Holafly eSIMs are one-off purchases for a single trip or destination (200+ available). Holafly Plans is an ongoing global subscription for people who are more or less always traveling.

Does Always On cost extra? No. It’s included automatically with every Holafly Plans subscription and keeps giving you 1GB of backup data a month across 150+ destinations even after you cancel.

Can I switch between Light and Unlimited? You’d need to cancel your current plan and purchase the other tier — there’s no in-place upgrade yet.

What if I don’t like it? Holafly backs Plans with a 6-month refund policy, which is more generous than most eSIM companies offer.

A deadly flash flood swept through Grand Canyon National Park in northern Arizona over the weekend. An active search-and-rescue operation is underway along the Colorado River, and parts of the inner canyon and South Rim are closed at this time.

Due to extreme damage and flash flooding in the Grand Canyon this past weekend, the National Park Service announced immediate closures of the following areas until further notice: Phantom Ranch, Phantom Ranch cabins and canteen and Bright Angel Campground. The entire North Kaibab Trail — from the North Kaibab Trailhead to Phantom Ranch — is also closed until further notice. The Silver and Black footbridges crossing the river have been affected as well.

For the latest trail and closure information, visit the park's Key Hiking Messages webpage.

A threat of severe weather still remains, and visitors are urged to exercise caution. Videos posted online by the Associated Press showed the destruction caused by the flooding. This devastating flash flood comes just a year after the Dragon Bravo wildfire forced the evacuation and closure of the North Rim in July 2025.

The closure of the inner canyon will allow the National Park Service and the Arizona Department of Public Safety to continue search-and-rescue operations. There are still visitors unaccounted for, and the NPS Investigative Services Branch is seeking the public’s assistance.

The flash flood significantly affected infrastructure in the canyon, including the Transcanyon Waterline, and, as a result, the visitor facilities at the South Rim are also affected.

Yes, it is safe to travel to portions of Grand Canyon National Park, but there are some restrictions that visitors should be aware of. We suggest bookmarking the park's main page, which lists updates and links to advisories.

The Places To Go page is full of helpful visitor information and maps.

The National Park Service has issued a closure notice for Monday, Aug. 31, at noon local time for the South Rim hotels located within Grand Canyon National Park due to damage to the Transcanyon Waterline. All water at the South Rim is delivered via the waterline, and additional reserves are running low. Only dry camping will be permitted at the South Rim.

It’s important to note that the park will remain open for day use, and food-and-beverage services at the South Rim will remain open (though some may reduce hours of operation).

As we’ve previously reported, the Transcanyon Waterline dates back to the 1960s, and the park has already invested $208 million in a multiyear rehabilitation project that isn't expected to be completed until 2027. The most recent update provided by Grand Canyon Lodges lists the hotels at the South Rim as projected to reopen on November 20, 2026.

Tusayan is the gateway to the South Rim of Grand Canyon National Park at the Route 64 entrance, and its hotels and restaurants remain fully operational and unaffected, as it's located outside the national park.

Until further notice, the Colorado River is closed to river traffic due to metal structures and debris entering the river, according to a notice from the National Park Service. River operations rangers are coordinating with visitors already in the canyon, and the Grand Canyon River Alert system is also sending advisories. If you have an upcoming river trip scheduled, you should contact the commercial outfitter that you booked with or the NPS River Permits office for trip-specific information.

#6289. Frontier Airlines Starts Selling First Class From $129. I Am Seriously Considering Booking It.

Frontier Airlines is now selling its new first class seats, with wider seating and no middle seats in the first two rows. Extra-legroom seating, USB-C power, and Starlink internet are also part of the cabin transformation. I welcome the investment, though a better seat will only get Frontier so far if the rest of the experience does not improve alongside it.

Installation is underway, with completion expected March 5, 2027. Reservations are open for travel beginning that day.

Promotional pricing requires purchasing the flight and bundle together by November 16, 2026, at 11:59 pm ET, for select nonstop domestic departures March 5–April 5, 2027. Availability is limited.

USB-C power is planned for the first eight rows. Both power and Starlink installations begin in 2027 and progress aircraft by aircraft throughout the year. Booking the new seat does not mean every other advertised improvement will be available on your flight.

For me, reliable internet and the ability to keep a laptop charged substantially determine how useful a flight is. A comfortable seat is welcome, but on a daytime trip I also must get work done…it is an essential part of the package.

I have to say, I’m quite excited about these developments.

As much as I loved warmed mixed nuts, a hot meal, and sparkling water saved with lime and ice in a glass…the Frontier network is respectable and a comfortable seat with Wi-Fi and power are more important. If Frontier can charge half or what American or United are asking on the same route, I’m totally up for flying Frontier more.

The bigger question is whether Frontier can persuade passengers to pay more and then give them a reason to come back.

A first class seat loses much of its appeal if a cancellation leaves you with poor alternatives or resolving an ordinary problem becomes an ordeal…two areas where traditional network carriers still have a huge advantage. Selling a premium product raises expectations even when the price is relatively low.

I do not expect Frontier to become a full-service airline simply because it installs eight larger seats. But I would expect the airline to understand that passengers purchasing those seats are buying some relief from the compromises associated with budget travel, again myself included.

That makes this an opportunity. If Frontier can offer a comfortable seat at a sensible total price and deliver dependable transportation and maybe a little bit more service than the “Big Front Seat” on Spirit Airlines, I think there is a market for it.

Frontier Airlines is moving forward with first class, and I welcome more choice at the front of the aircraft. The new seats could make the airline more attractive to passengers who value comfort but remain sensitive to price, like me. Even the extra legroom seats are something I would consider, with Starlink being an even bigger game-changer.

While I would happily try it, the real test will be whether Frontier delivers an experience that makes me want to book it again. A larger seat with Starlink can get someone through the door…but Frontier must deliver that.

#6287. American Airlines Bringing Back First Class “Mini-Meals” On Shorter Flights

American Airlines reportedly plans to bring back “light bites” in first class on flights of 700–899 miles, beginning between New York and Chicago. I love this concept. A shorter flight does not require an elaborate meal, but something fresh would be a welcome improvement over another trip through the snack basket.

JonNYC reports that American will restore its light-bites concept on shorter domestic first class flights, starting with New York–Chicago service (0r flights from New York and Chicago).

AA:"Light bites”/mini-meals coming back to short haul domestic first class flights 700-899 milesStarting on NYC/ORD.

We do not yet have a firm launch date, menus, or a detailed rollout schedule.  American’s published dining page still lists a snack basket on flights of 500–899 miles during meal times, with meal service on longer flights. The proposed change would give passengers at the upper end of that snack-basket range something more substantial.

A full meal is not necessary on every flight, but there is a lot of room between a hot entrée with multiple accompaniments and a bag of pretzels. A ramekin of warmed mixed nuts followed by a small fresh plate would be a very fitting compromise.

Think small dishes like a bowl of fruit in the morning or hummus with vegetables in the afternoon. The point is that a modest offering can still feel thoughtful and satisfy a bit of hunger…it also adds a premium touch that would nicely distinguish American from Delta and United (Alaska Airlines, to its credit, already serves meals on shorter flights).

A recent example: I flew from Boston to Chicago on AA, a flight of 867 miles and blocked at over 2.5 hours. No real food in first class, just a snack basket. A light meal would have been very appreciated and I was hungry.

There is something frustrating about boarding a first class flight around meal times and discovering that the route falls just short of the meal threshold…so-called “exception markets” used to exist, but have been cut on AA (oddly, except for Chicago – Denver).

My hope is that American focuses on quality, though I already give AA credit for better food than on Delta and United.

I am certainly quick to criticize American when the experience falls short, but I have also enjoyed some very good meals onboard. That is worth applauding, as is this change. A larger seat remains the primary reason many people buy domestic first class. Still, when airlines ask passengers to pay a premium, the experience should reflect some care beyond the dimensions of the seat, especially when AA will be charging a lot more than Frontier.

American Airlines reportedly plans to restore light bites in first class on flights of 700–899 miles, beginning on New York / Chicago routes. The timing and actual food remain to be seen, but I am enthusiastic about the direction. This is a sensible and competitive improvement, and I hope American gets it right and expands it.

#6285. United Airlines Finally Plans Boeing 757-300 Makeover With Seatback Screens And Bigger Bins

United Airlines plans to give its Boeing 757-300 fleet a long-overdue cabin update, adding larger overhead bins, entertainment screens at every seat, and power throughout the cabin. These aircraft have needed attention for years and were always included in the United Next refresh plan, though I am somewhat surprised to see United keep these workhorses in the fleet.

United Airlines 757-300 aircraft will be modified in accordance with the United’s “United Next” strategy, which includes installation of new Boeing Space Bins, Panasonic Audio Video On Demand (AVOD), In Flight Entertainment at every seat location, full cabin In-Seat Power Supply System (ISPS), new class dividers and cabin headers, and new UAL branding elements. Additionally, all seats and monuments will be refreshed throughout the cabin.

United:“United Airlines 757-300 aircraft will be modified in accordance with the United's "United Next" strategy, which includes installation of new Boeing Space Bins, Panasonic Audio Video On Demand (AVOD), In Flight Entertainment at every seat location, full cabin In-Seat…

As I mentioned above, the surprise is not that United is refreshing its entire narrwobody fleet, which it has promised for years now, but that it is actually moving forward with the 757-300s rather than phasing them out. However, I also understand that an A321neo or 737 MAX is not necessarily a direct replacement for this workhorse.

My understanding is that one reason this project took longer to get moving was the lack of a certified larger-bin option for this particular aircraft. United had to work through that certification hurdle rather than simply order an existing installation, which puts the delay in context.

United listed just 21 Boeing 757-300s in its year-end 2025 fleet disclosure, each with 234 seats. Undertaking a specialized modification for a fleet that small is a more substantial commitment than fitting the same equipment across hundreds of aircraft. For passengers, however, the size of the subfleet is beside the point. If your flight is operated by a 757-300, the overhead storage and cabin condition are part of your United experience.

More useful bin space should make boarding less stressful: currently there are far too many bags that must be gate checked because the smaller overhead bins force larger (but standard) carry-on bags to be placed on their sides.

I will also be happy to see entertainment screens included throughout the aircraft. When traveling with my children, individual screens are especially useful.

JonNYC also mentions power and it will be great to have USB-C, but the aircraft already have universal A/C power outlets in every cabin.

But what JonNYC does not mention and I consider most important is that these aircraft will get Starlink. Currently, most 757-300s still have an ancient Panasonic Wi-Fi system that often does not work. I specifically avoid the 757-300 for this reason and have been burned almost every time I have flown it with non-operable Wi-Fi. Some 757-300s have been upgraded with Viasat, but I am unwilling to fly on the 753s unless absolutely necessary. The new cabins will be welcomed, but Starlink is the most important upgrade.

I do not object to an aircraft simply because it is older: Delta has shown that a 30-year-old aircraft with mood lighting, fast Wi-Fi, and seatback screens can feel just as comfortable as a more modern aircraft. Refreshed seating and better amenities can change that experience substantially, even when the aircraft itself has been flying for decades.

This investment suggests United sees a continuing role for the 757-300 for many years in the future.

The Boeing 757-300 is finally in line for the kind of cabin attention it has long needed. Larger bins, seatback entertainment, and Starlink Wi-Fi will make a noticeable difference. I figured these aircraft would just be retired, but it appears they will fly the “Friendly Skies” for many years to come.

#6284. What’s Your Airport Dwell Time? A Metric Businesses Think A Lot About

Dwell time, simply, is how long you spend in an airport, or airport space, before a flight. For most people, it’s not something they’ve ever actively really thought about.

For businesses in air travel and airports, like lounge operators, credit card companies or airlines, it’s one of the main things they think about. So what’s yours and what does it say about you?

Well, a lot. More importantly, the tracking of that dwell time has contributed to quite a lot of innovation in lounges and airports, with hopefully much more to come.

Build it and they will come. Who knew Kevin Costner knew so much about lounges?! In truth, if someone builds a lounge, everyone will come and ensuring it’s a good experience is an art form requiring math. Crowds can be hard to predict and most lounges are “too” full these days.

Knowing the average dwell time of a customer, and even a specific customer profile is one of the best tools lounges have to predict the flows of customers, including how much they’ll need to stock in food and drinks and everything else during peak times.

Even outside of lounges, knowing how long an air traveler spends in the airport is vital to understanding what kind of businesses, restaurants or concessions to offer. There’s a reason grab and go places do really, really well and get away with charging $12 for water.

Surprisingly to some, top tier frequent flyers typically have a really low dwell time compared to lower ranks or leisure travelers.

If an airline knows their lounge is full of top tiers that day, they can expect many people who won’t stay long. Whereas, if it’s a day with full flights and mostly leisure travel passengers, you can predict people will dwell far longer.

It makes sense. If you’re not used to the delights of a great airport lounge you come earlier, stay longer and take advantage of more. You also have less confidence in timings of the check in and security process, so you pad time in, in addition to the natural, “treat yourself” vibes.

If you do it all the time, every minute not in the airport is often seen as the win, so lounges are just a place to quickly reset and refresh before carrying on.

The first time I experienced a true first class lounge I think I got to the airport at the earliest possible interval. I had hours in there and of course, tried everything.

But I’ve been very lucky, I’ve experienced most lounges many times, been spoiled by the best many times, and unless there’s a real wow factor moment, I’m happiest spending as little time waiting in an airport as possible. Don’t get me wrong, I still indulge from time to time, but I’ve seen a huge dip in my own dwell average.

As I strolled through T2 at Heathrow this week en route to the United Club, it occurred to me that most of my recent lounge visits averaged about 30 minutes in total. In that 30 minutes I’d say I have a maximum of one drink, often little or no food, and mostly take advantage of the wifi and nice calm facilities.

I’ve gotten my time from curb to security at Heathrow down to a decent science and I like it that way. At other airports with even more predictable security and check in patterns, I’ll shave even more time off, often leaving no time for lounges at all.

And this raises a fair question: if everyone could truly model out their time from curb to airside, would they spend as long? Things like TSA PreCheck and CLEAR have been monumental in adding a layer of certainty to this process and I’d expect we’ll see more of it. Will more passengers change habits as they have better confidence in making their flight while cutting it fine?

Now of course, all bets are off when I travel with my kids. And that’s kind of the point. We think we’re very unique in our travel habits, but there are many variables of our travels which drop us into a fairly predictable pattern … and dwell time.

When lounge access is a marquee benefit of being a frequent flyer, but most top frequent flyers hardly leave any time for lounge dwelling, is that a real selling point?

In response, we’ve seen really clever pivots lately, including from Air Canada and Capital One. Each brand has created curated “grab and go” offerings in their lounges or lounge-like areas to offer passengers complimentary things which have tangible value — a nitro cold brew latte, or a nice pastry — for “free”, which they’re totally able to take on the road with them.

That’s a huge departure from the days of lounges with signs everywhere saying no outside food and drinks and no removing food or drinks from the lounge. People never paid attention anyway, and this now just creates a formalized and better thought out approach to catering to all traveler needs.

The big question is: what’s next for adding value to a travelers airport journey? Be sure to share your lounge and travel habits as well.

There is no shortage of ways to redeem your points and miles for travel to Europe. With most flights being overnight, booking a lie-flat seat is an excellent way to ensure you arrive rested and refreshed on the continent.

Points and miles enthusiasts usually need to choose between paying high redemption rates or high surcharges. Programs like Delta SkyMiles charge just $5.60 in taxes and fees for business-class flights to Europe but expect up to 500,000 miles per person for flights as short as seven hours on peak dates.

Many European programs have much lower redemption rates, such as British Airways Club, which charges just 88,000 Avios for a one-way, off-peak flight to London from the Northeast. The trade-off is you will need to stump up almost $500 in taxes, fees and surcharges to BA.

The Scandinavian Airlines EuroBonus program charges just 60,000 EuroBonus points for a one-way, SAS-operated Business Bonus award between North America and Europe. The cherry on top? You'll need to pay just $5.60 in taxes and fees. Although this loyalty currency has traditionally been difficult to earn, thanks to the new Rove transfer option, you can fly to Europe for less than the price of a cup of coffee in taxes and fees by redeeming miles.

Related: Earning 28 miles per dollar: How a 2-night New York City hotel stay earned me enough miles to fly to Europe using Rove

Here's how to do it and what my experience was like.

SAS doesn't add carrier-imposed surcharges to awards on flights it operates, making SAS EuroBonus one of the best-value Rove transfer partners for business-class travel to Europe.

SAS flies nonstop to Copenhagen Airport (CPH) from the following U.S. gateways, although some routes are seasonal:

SAS also flies nonstop from Newark to Oslo Airport (OSL) and Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN).

Related: SAS has brought back European Business class on short-haul flights

Business Bonus seats at the fixed 60,000-point rate were strictly limited and were not available on every route or date I searched. When they were unavailable, SAS displayed regular fares that could be paid with points at a much higher rate, so flexible dates helped a lot.

Rove miles transfer to EuroBonus points at a 1:1 ratio, with a 2,000-mile minimum and transfers in increments of 100 miles. My transfer posted instantly, though Rove says transfers usually complete within one day.

Transfers can't be reversed, so the golden rule applies here: Find award space you're happy with before you move a single mile.

SAS award flights booked on the website must currently be reserved at least three days before departure. The SAS app allows closer-in bookings, but for reservations made within three days of departure, the EuroBonus member must be traveling.

Taxes and fees were higher on the way back. When I checked, a SAS business-class award from Copenhagen to the U.S. required about $95 one-way.

Related: A game of thrones: Flying business class on Scandinavian Airlines' A321LR from Copenhagen to Washington

EuroBonus isn't the only option to redeem your Rove miles to fly to Europe. Other transfer partners can be used, but the combination of redemption rates plus taxes, fees and surcharges is not as attractive as EuroBonus:

Related: How to avoid paying fuel surcharges when redeeming points and miles

My journey to Europe began by purchasing a tall latte from Starbucks at ATL for $6.16, including Georgia sales tax, more than the taxes and fees I paid for my business-class flight.

I then used the Sky Priority check-in for my flight to Copenhagen, which allowed me to check two bags, each up to 70 pounds.

SAS business-class tickets to Europe include access to Delta Sky Club lounges. SAS departs from Concourse F, one of the two international concourses at Atlanta Airport, so I headed to the Sky Club in this concourse.

Related: A posh Delta One lounge is coming to Atlanta

It featured an outdoor terrace, which was a great place for planespotting and soaking up the Georgia sunshine.

A kindly staff member who noticed my photo-taking gave me a tip that there was a newer and more luxurious Sky Club in Concourse D I could access on the same ticket. Since I still had several hours before my flight, I headed over there.

It was a big, bright room with floor-to-ceiling windows on both sides looking out over the airfield, and the green and teal decor was a nod to Atlanta's "City in a Forest" nickname.

Based on my visit, I would recommend heading to Concourse D if you have time; I preferred its newer, larger space.

Related: Inside Delta's brand-new Sky Club in Atlanta, its nicest one yet

There were plenty of hot and cold food options available, which is ideal for anyone heading to Europe and wanting to maximize their rest on their flight.

Despite being busy during the late afternoon and early evening, the bartenders happily served up sparkling wine, beers and soft drinks and well as whipping up cocktails and chatting to guests about their travel plans.

After taking advantage of priority boarding for business passengers, I boarded the SAS Airbus A350-900, which had 40 business-class seats in a 1-2-1 layout, so every passenger had direct aisle access.

The cabin had a calm, understated palette of charcoal gray seat shells with brushed silver trim and blue-flecked gray fabric, with a tan, leather-look panel lining each side console to warm it up.

The bedding was already at my seat when I boarded, wrapped in plastic. It came from Dux, the Swedish bedmaker that was SAS's official comfort partner at the time, and included a gray and white pinstriped duvet and two pillows.

The amenity kit was a limited-edition one for SAS’s 80th anniversary. It came in a navy zip pouch with the airline’s 80 logo on the front. Inside was a matching navy eye mask, earplugs and a dental kit, plus lip balm and hand cream from Swedish skincare brand Muro Scents.

A pair of SAS-branded over-ear headphones hung on a hook in the side console. There was a universal power outlet and a USB port right next to it, and the seat itself was controlled from a touchscreen panel, including lumbar support.

I was more interested in sleep than cinema on my flight to Denmark, but the 18.5-inch touchscreen had a solid selection of recent releases, including "The Devil Wears Prada 2."

The drinks list was where SAS leans hardest into its Scandinavian roots.

Alongside Charles Heidsieck Brut Reserve Champagne, there was a hazy IPA brewed by Danish brewery Mikkeller in collaboration with SAS; two SAS-exclusive spirits, Herno Old Tom Gin and High Coast whisky from Sweden; and a cocktail menu that included the SASmopolitan.

For my Atlanta departure, the menu had a definite Georgia flavor. The starter options were grilled peaches wrapped in prosciutto with mozzarella and balsamic pearls or seared ahi tuna. Main courses included smoked beef short rib with stone-ground grits from Georgia's Riverview Farms, a hot honey-glazed chicken thigh and goat cheese and apple ravioli.

I chose the ahi tuna, which was a light and fresh start to the meal, with a hearty slice of sourdough bread on the side.

For the main course, I went for the beef short rib, an indulgent and delicious option with super-tender beef and creamy grits.

With a fairly short flight time and a full stomach, I skipped dessert, reclined my seat fully flat and settled in for the night.

The crew set up a snack bar for business-class passengers who got hungry during the flight, but most focused on getting a good night's rest.

I slept right through breakfast (the crew had asked at dinner whether I wanted to be woken) and arrived refreshed and ready to explore the charming city of Copenhagen.

After years of having to choose between high redemption rates and high surcharges, booking through SAS EuroBonus could be the ultimate sweet spot to Europe.

I've flown plenty of business-class products across the Atlantic, and SAS offered a very respectable experience on the A350 with friendly staff, direct aisle access, comfortable bedding and some fun Scandic touches.

Joining Rove costs nothing, and you can earn 1,500 bonus miles when you sign up through TPG's link. As an added bonus, new users can earn an additional 5,000 miles after making their first hotel booking of $500 or more with code "BRIANKELLY500".

I'd much rather pay $5.60 for a lie-flat seat to Europe than a cup of coffee. How about you?

#6282. United Airlines CEO Talks Starlink In Veterans Day Message

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby used his Veterans Day message to thank the 8,500 veterans who work at the airline. But before turning to their service, he spent a substantial part of the message discussing Starlink, winning customers from competitors, and his belief that United is the best airline in the world. The opening offers another glimpse into what Kirby sees as the opportunity ahead in 2027.

I typically share Kirby’s internal Veterans Day message each year (he also posted publicly on LinkedIN). His appreciation for military service and his affection for the United States are familiar themes. This year, though, he began with a thank-you for the summer operation and a look ahead at how better Wi-Fi might persuade passengers to switch airlines.

Happy Veterans Day everyone. Before I start on my Veterans Day message, I want to thank everyone for a really incredible summer. All the hard work you do. There was a lot of weather this summer, but the United team just did a great job so thank you. I also want to tell you how excited I am for 2027. In 2027 we’re going have a unique advantage in Starlink. And what that means is we’re gonna have a lot of customers who are loyal to other airlines today try us because of Starlink and I can already can hear this from customers. What’s going to happen is I hope they’re going to realize that United really is the best airline in the world when they come try United. We’re gonna be able to get those customers to come to United because of Starlink but to stay with United because everything else United is better. So thank you in advance for what you’re gonna do to win new brand loyal customers in 2027 for us at United.

But what I really wanted to do today is thank the 8,500 veterans that work here at United Airlines. I think all of you know that I am deeply patriotic. I love this country. I feel fortunate to have been born in this country and think it’s the greatest country in the history of the planet, but that wouldn’t be the case if it wasn’t for all the veterans who work at United but all the other veterans and the people that serve today. So to all the veterans not just at United, but around the world who have served to put their lives on the line to keep this country free and great, thank you for your service. Thank you for everything that you’ve done. And today when you’re out working and you see a veteran, and I’m sure you will because there’s so many United, give them a special thank you for their service. So to everyone at United, thank you for everything that you’ve done. And the veterans, a special thank you on Veteran’s Day and I look forward to seeing you in the friendly skies.

The commercial opening is an unusual preface to a Veterans Day tribute, though Kirby explicitly separates it from the message that follows. That makes sense considering he is addressing all employees and using the opportunity to discuss more than one subject. Still, his emphasis is revealing.

Kirby sees Starlink as a reason for passengers loyal to other airlines to give United a try, which is likely true. The more ambitious part is his expectation that the rest of the experience will persuade them to stay.

Reliable, fast internet can absolutely influence my booking decision. If I need to work during a flight, connectivity is more important than modest differences in the seat or meal and I’m hardly alone.

The second proposition is true, though certainly easier said than done. A passenger attracted by Starlink still has to navigate the airport, interact with the crew, and arrive at the destination. A great internet connection may get someone to book once. How United handles that journey, especially when something goes wrong, will help determine whether the passenger returns.

I remain unconvinced that there is one universally “best” airline. But Kirby is giving his employees a clear assignment: use the opportunity created by Starlink to earn repeat business. That is indeed a useful objective and to Untied’s credit, it improving operational performance and overall onboard product are giving front-line staff the means to deliver.

Turning to Veterans Day, Kirby’s message is direct. He credits those who have served with protecting the country he loves and asks employees to thank the veterans they encounter at work. I appreciate that practical request and will do the same today in my own interactions (I’m not flying, though).

Gratitude does not require agreement with every military deployment or government decision. We can (and should) scrutinize those decisions while appreciating the people asked to carry them out and the sacrifices their service entails.

Kirby’s Veterans Day message combines a familiar expression of patriotism with an enthusiastic commercial outlook for 2027. His expectation that Starlink will bring new passengers through the door does indeed create a golden opportunity for United. Whether United earns their loyalty will depend on what happens beyond the Wi-Fi connection.

But today’s central message deserves its own acknowledgment. To the veterans at United Airlines and elsewhere, thank you for your service.

#6281. New Credit Card Sets Annual Fee Dynamically, Based On Benefit Usage

Among savvy Redditors and credit card blogs, there’s a common thread with many recent credit card changes. “It feels like a coupon book” is often the consumer reaction, particularly as annual fees rise as justification for an increasing number of partner offer benefits, which if consumed in entirety could lead to more value.

Since many people simply won’t use all the benefits and partner offers being baked into the card, people increasingly feel like the annual fee rises are getting too steep. In a bold move, a new card launched today which offers a flexible annual fee, based only on the benefits you actually use.

Signed up for a card named after a precious or semi precious metal and shocked by the $450-$695 fee? You’re not alone.

To get your money back from such a fee, you’d need to take advantage of regular lounge access at airports, utilize your TSA PreCheck/Global Entry credit, maximize every monthly dining or entertainment credit and sign up for every other fee credit, which often requires a purchase.

To quell this issue, the new card is effectively a build your own card, card.

Despite the innovation, the card draws on the historical concept of the coupon book, where you only pay for the offers you tear out and redeem. The annual fee starts at zero, but as you actually redeem the cards benefits, you get billed accordingly. Your fee can be zero, or as high as $10,000 per year.

Done right, you can end up paying $650 in annual fees for about $800 worth of stuff, some of which you wanted and most of which, about $700 worth, you didn’t really want or need, but felt compelled to get, just because it’s there.

This model allows you to really dive into the classic coupon book, feeling like you’re really tearing offers out of the page, and simply leaving the ones you’re not using in the book. You’re only paying for the ones you rip out, but when there’s so many offers to choose from, the book just feels so compelling.

Obviously, it’s April 1st and no such card is coming to the market (yet, lol), but hopefully this light hearted amusement has been a helpful exercise in framing the true value you’re really extracting from your premium credit card, or conversely, the lack thereof.

Consider the things you’d actually purchase without the “offer” prompt and if that number still adds up to be more than the annual fee, you’re doing it right. If it doesn’t…
