#6257. ‘Not Served In Exit Rows’: United Airlines Passenger Refused A Drink, Gets 5,000 Miles

An exit-row passenger was flying to Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport (SJU). While on the flight, the passenger asked for an alcoholic drink and was refused service. The flight attendant said that such beverages are not served to exit-row passengers.

After other Reddit users told the passenger that the flight attendant was not following Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) policy, they filed a complaint with the airline. United apologized and added 5,000 miles to the passenger's MileagePlus account.

In the Reddit post titled "No adult drinks in exit row," the passenger explains that they were flying to SJU for the evening before their birthday. To celebrate their vacation, the passenger tried to purchase an alcoholic drink on the United flight and was disappointed to be denied service. The passenger initially thought that the flight attendant was correct, writing, "bad time to learn that alcohol is not served in exit rows."

The passenger then gave three updates to the many others who commented. The first said that they had made a complaint. The second explained that being drunk wasn't why they were refused, as the drink they ordered would have been the first of the day.

"I get that drunk passengers are a menace," they wrote.

Finally, the passenger said they received 5,000 United MileagePlus miles.

Simple Flying contacted United, but it said it will not comment on the matter.

The compensation comes because the flight attendant broke United's alcohol sales policy. Alcoholic drinks are not sold to those under 21 years old or those who are already intoxicated. Furthermore, the FAA has no ban on serving alcohol in exit rows. As a result, there is no reason that the passenger should have been denied service.

There are rules about exit row travel that frequent flyers will know. Passengers in these rows must be at least 15 years old, physically mobile, and able to read and understand safety briefings. They also must be able to respond to oral instructions in English or the crew's operational language. Finally, passengers in the exit row can't have other responsibilities that would conflict with them helping in an emergency. Examples include that they are traveling with small children or service animals that are caring for another passenger.

In addition to being able to help in an emergency, they must also be willing to do so. In the US, this must be confirmed verbally.

Delta and other carriers must start pre-departure service earlier so galley items are stowed prior to aircraft movement.

"With 5k miles, nothing. Just keep earning more," wrote one Reddit user on a different thread, underlining that the miles given to the passenger impacted by the denial of service is an apology and a gesture rather than true compensation.

Having the 5,000 miles contribute toward a larger spend is not the only way the passenger could benefit from the apology. They could use MileagePlus Merchandise Awards to shop for electronics, household items, and jewelry, although their options would be limited to just 5,000 miles. The only item currently available in the 3,000 to 5,000-mile range is a Gaiam Sidekick Waist Pack, costing 4,800 miles. This pack has a retail price of around $20. Other rewards, like hotels, car hire, and cruises, will also be out of reach with so few miles.

However, some ways to use small amounts of miles are no longer available. For example, United formerly had a program called MagsforMiles, where passengers could use their miles to take out magazine subscriptions. This program has now been shut down.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

I just don't order alcohol if I'm in the exit row. If something happens and I can't get my stuff together to open the exit then it's bad for everyone.

Also, one cannot be of a size where they need to use a seatbelt extender. I'm lucky I found out the easy/not embarrassing way.

Free adult bevys on my AA flights in the exit row.

JetBlue’s newest premium seats are ready for takeoff.

The airline just unveiled its new domestic first-class product called “BlueFirst.” It’s set to debut on flights next month, but TPG got a sneak peek at the seats ahead of the launch.

The new first-class seats will take up the first few rows on most of JetBlue’s planes, going forward.

Eventually, JetBlue flyers will see first-class on all of the carrier’s aircraft — except for jets that already have its lie-flat Mint cabin.

And with complimentary upgrades on the horizon for JetBlue’s Mosaic elite members, the addition of BlueFirst should offer TrueBlue loyalists some enticing new status perks in the near future.

Read more: JetBlue announces first-class upgrades, new elite benefits for 2027

JetBlue plans to offer three — or four — rows of BlueFirst, depending on the plane.

Like most domestic first-class products in the U.S., the seats are arranged in a 2-by-2 configuration.

JetBlue outfitted its BlueFirst seats with a handful of thoughtful touches, such as “flex foam” cushioning from mattress and bedding company Tuft and Needle.

The headrest also sports a special BlueFirst logo.

Beyond that, expect a host of seating upgrades from JetBlue’s core cabin. These seats have cocktail trays, extra storage and a large tray table with a personal device holder.

The 13-inch seatback screens are the first in JetBlue’s fleet to offer Bluetooth connectivity, which means passengers will be able to connect their wireless headphones, such as Apple AirPods.

The screens also offer a unique twist on ordering drinks inflight. “Mixologist Mode” allows BlueFirst flyers to customize their cocktail order with a base and mixers.

JetBlue is also rolling out a new “soft product” around the BlueFirst seats, including a new line of inflight food, drinks and amenities.

While the carrier won’t offer hot meals (no ovens!) on its domestic aircraft, there’s an array of creatively assembled bento box meals. Options range from sesame beef noodles with crispy wontons and Szechuan dip to tortellini pasta salad and a pastrami sandwich (and more).

JetBlue has a strong track record for its on-board food. And while the lack of ovens probably means its BlueFirst food won’t stack up to what you’d get on a long-haul Mint flight, the spread the airline showed off this week looks impressive — even if it will be served chilled.

BlueFirst service will also include a new array of wines curated by New York-based Parcelle Wine — plus a fresh lineup of amenities, glassware, and coasters designed by a local artist.

JetBlue’s new first-class product will debut on Dec. 8, on its service from Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) to Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport (FLL).

The airline has dozens of routes already slated for the new seats, which will continue to roll out across its fleet as JetBlue retrofits its planes.

Among the biggest winners in its first-class launch: JetBlue frequent flyers with elite status.

All TrueBlue Mosaic members will be eligible for complimentary, space-available upgrades.

Plus, customers who carry JetBlue’s top-end premium credit card will also be able to join the upgrade queue.

High-level Mosaics will also be eligible to use their confirmable upgrade certificates on BlueFirst (However, you can also still use those to upgrade to Mint, which will remain the airline’s top seat).

You can read all about JetBlue’s new upgrade policy and updated Mosaic benefits in our latest story about the TrueBlue program.

The launch of BlueFirst marks a new chapter for JetBlue’s on-board product.

The carrier began flying at the turn of the century with all-economy cabins.

It first waded into the premium space in 2014, when it launched Mint. Now, it's time to add domestic first-class to the mix — a cabin executives described Wednesday as “very JetBlue.”

‘Cheap chic’: How JetBlue’s first 25 years of flying helped reshape US aviation

It comes as U.S. travelers are about to see a wave of new first-class seats hit the market — from JetBlue to budget airlines Frontier and Allegiant.

There are some drawbacks to JetBlue’s new seats at the front of the plane.

To make room for the new recliner seats, the carrier’s long-celebrated economy legroom will shrink on some planes.

There’s also no divider between first-class and coach — and, as we noted, the meals won’t be hot.

But BlueFirst will certainly raise the bar on JetBlue's top-level service on domestic flights, and serve as a worthy complement to its popular Mint product.

Also, the chance for complimentary upgrades will be a key new perk for Mosaic elites.

And for an airline hoping to give customers more reasons to prioritize its TrueBlue loyalty program, the new seats could prove a meaningful addition for years to come.

#6255. SeaWorld Parks Promo Codes November 2026

Marriott Coupon CodesYou never forget your first dolphin encounter—and for many kids across the country, that often happens at SeaWorld. The beloved oceanarium puts the “amusement” in amusement parks: orcas leaping in the air, floorless rollercoasters named after sea monsters, and even aquarium sleepovers. With parks in Orlando, San Diego, San Antonio, and Abu Dhabi, SeaWorld’s aquatic allure has no bounds. SeaWorld is a top choice when it comes to taking the family out for some educational fun.

Established in 1964 by four UCLA graduates, SeaWorld began in San Diego with 22 acres, six attractions, and a handful of sea lions and dolphins (beloved orca whale Shamu arrived at the party a year later). In the early 2000s, the parks expanded with thrill rides and rollercoasters, as well as Discovery Cove, allowing visitors to interact with marine animals like bottlenose dolphins. Over the course of its history, SeaWorld has rescued over 40,000 animals and, through the SeaWorld and Busch Gardens Conservation Fund, donated over $19 million to global projects, from restoring coral reefs to preventing coastal erosion. If you want your little ones to have a whale of a time, here are the best SeaWorld Parks promo codes, discounts, and deals.

Take advantage of SeaWorld's Black Friday discounts. Save up to 60% on tickets, fun cards, and passes. Save over 50% on a single-day ticket to SeaWorld San Diego ($65 instead of $130) and enjoy increased flexibility if you visit before March 31, 2027. Combine it with the All-Day Dining option for $40, and you won't have to worry about buying meals. You can also save 40% on a 2027 Fun Card and take advantage of unlimited free visits to SeaWorld San Diego now through 2027 ($78 from $130).

SeaWorld expresses its gratitude for the service of military members through the Waves of Honor program, which grants any US active-duty military, activated or drilling reservist, or National Guardsman one complimentary admission per year, and tickets for as many as three direct dependents. Military personnel can also enjoy a 50% off discount on up to six SeaWorld Orlando single-day tickets, plus a Silver Annual Pass at SeaWorld Orlando (unlimited admission with no blockout dates for 12 months) for $161 instead of $279. Those who can take advantage of this offer will need to verify their identity via ID.Me.

For military personnel who have completed their service, SeaWorld is offering 50% off single-day tickets at SeaWorld Orlando, plus the same Silver Annual Pass discount that active-duty military members get to enjoy. To take advantage of this offer, verify with ID.Me.

If you’ve got a preschooler, give them the gift of maximum aquarium time. At SeaWorld San Antonio, kids under the age of five can enjoy free, unlimited admission to SeaWorld until January 2027, plus unlimited visits to Aquatica for only $39—just be sure to register before the offer expires on May 30. Preschool Cards are limited to Texas residents only.

Because SeaWorld is dedicated to research and education, the theme park offers certified K–12 teachers in Florida free admission. The SeaWorld Florida Teacher Card is valid for unlimited admission to SeaWorld Orlando through September 2, 2027. All teachers have to do is pre-register on ID.Me with a Department of Education (DOE) number. Plus, Florida Teacher Card holders have the option to add Aquatica Orlando for only $49.99.

If you find yourself visiting the dolphins often, consider investing in an annual pass for the lowest cost per visit. Annual passes often include perks like free guest tickets and discounts on food and merchandise. During the sale, prices for passes are reduced for new members: Save up to 15% on the Bronze Pass, 20% on Silver, 25% on Gold, and 30% on Platinum. Using a SeaWorld Parks promo code annual pass deal can pay for itself in just two visits.

To make sure your SeaWorld discount applies correctly, verify the expiration date; many SeaWorld coupons are time-sensitive. Check if the code is park-specific (for example, a SeaWorld Orlando promo code may not work for San Diego). And finally, ensure you are not trying to stack, let’s say, an AAA discount with a military offer, as most SeaWorld discounts cannot be combined.

#6254. JetBlue is Launching a New Domestic First Class—and We Got a First Look

Flying domestic with JetBlue just got an upgrade. On Wednesday, November 11, the airline introduced BlueFirst, a brand-new domestic first class product, ahead of its debut flight on December 8. The cabin is a dedicated section in the first three rows, arranged two-by-two (read: no middle seats). It will be installed across the airline's fleet on planes that do not already have a Mint business class cabin, bringing a domestic first class to the shorter routes for which JetBlue is more commonly known. As Stephanie Evans Greene, the airline’s senior vice president of marketing and brand, tells Condé Nast Traveler, the idea is "premium, but not pretentious."

BlueFirst will begin rolling out across JetBlue’s fleet in early December, beginning with the carrier’s daily Boston–Fort Lauderdale flight and soon followed by its popular Fort Lauderdale–New York LaGuardia route.

The new cabin is a big shift for JetBlue, an airline that for most of its 26 years in business flew economy seats only. The one exception is Mint, a lie-flat business class available on the airline's transcontinental and transatlantic routes, like New York to Los Angeles and London. To be clear: BlueFirst is not a version of Mint, and the two will never appear on the same plane. Mint planes keep Mint, and BlueFirst goes on every other aircraft. Where Mint is a bed, BlueFirst is a recliner, built for the shorter leisure routes that make up most of JetBlue's network.

To test out the BlueFirst product, we checked out the first aircraft with the new cabins installed on the ground at New York—JFK. Here's everything travelers should know before booking.

The first three rows of the plane will be dedicated to BlueFirst, with 12 seats in total.

As for the seat itself, the first thing that will stand out to travelers is just how much more space there is. BlueFirst has only three rows—12 seats total—and each seat is about three inches wider than a standard economy seat, with room to spare in every direction. The seat is spacious enough to hold a passenger and a laptop bag next to them (or a large purse, in my case), and the space in front is just as generous, with up to seven extra inches of legroom compared with JetBlue's regular Main seats. It reclines five inches too, though the recline takes a bit of pressure (hold the button and push back on the seat firmly). Press the button again, and the seat pops right back up. In true JetBlue fashion—this is, after all, the airline that built its name on being the un-stuffy one—there's no curtain cutting the BlueFirst cabin off from the rest of the plane.

Mattress company Tuft & Needle designed the seat cushion using T&N Flex foam.

The seat cushion is made with Tuft & Needle's T&N Flex foam (yes, the mattress company), developed just for JetBlue. It's squishy enough to comfortably sink into, and it responds as you shift, in both the bottom cushion and the backrest. The adjustable headrest also has wings that fold in to cradle your head. "I'll go on record and say I think they're some of the most comfortable recline seats that are out there in domestic first class," Greene says.

BlueFirst passengers receive a blanket and an amenity kit with socks, earbuds, mouthwash, and OSEA Malibu skincare products.

Aside from the bigger, more comfortable seat, BlueFirst gives travelers a slew of other perks. At every seat, there's a 13.3-inch screen with Bluetooth for personal earbuds, USB-A, USB-C, and a regular outlet, plus JetBlue's free Wi-Fi. The overhead bins above the cabin are reserved for BlueFirst passengers, so boarding doesn't come with the usual scramble for space, and each large bifold tray table has a stand for your phone or tablet. Travelers also get a blanket and an amenity kit with socks, earbuds, mouthwash, and OSEA Malibu skincare products, including a lip balm, hand cream, and the fan-favorite calming pulse point oil.

What's more, the perks start before passengers even get on the plane: BlueFirst comes with priority check-in, a faster security lane at more than 30 airports, and Group 1 boarding. Most BlueFirst fares come with two free checked bags—even BlueFirst Base, the cheapest of the three, includes one checked bag.

The dining options in BlueFirst depend on how long your flight is. A bento-inspired box is served on flights of 899 miles or more, with an entrée, a side, and a dessert. The exact menu changes based on the route. Dinner might be a tortellini pasta salad with marinated green olives, a pastrami sandwich with a citrusy cabbage salad, or sesame noodles with crispy wontons and a Szechuan dip. The desserts are a highlight: the pasta comes with a carrot cake with a caramel icing top that's deliciously moist (my personal favorite), and there are colorful macarons and a pistachio chocolate cake on other menus. Breakfast runs from hazelnut-ricotta crêpes to a sweet potato and bean bowl with guacamole and hot sauce, a poached pear, and blueberry chia pudding. There are also kosher, vegan, and gluten-free versions of the boxes.

Drinks in this section of the cabin deserve their own mention, because BlueFirst's come with a twist you won't find on other US airlines. Everything is ordered right from the seatback screen in Mixologist Mode, which lets you build your own cocktail (or mocktail) instead of choosing from a list. You start with a base—a spirit, a soft drink, coffee, a mixer—and add up to four items in total from the full drink menu. The crew then brings the ingredients right to your separate pop-out cocktail tray, and you mix it yourself. There's a limit of two drinks per order, but once the first round lands, you can start the next. The drinks come in real glassware from Fable, on handmade watercolor coasters by New York-based illustrator Danielle Rose Fisher. For anyone not playing bartender, there's also wine from Parcelle, coffee from Cometeer and Joe Coffee, and Smith Teamaker teas.

The new cabin will first roll out on JetBlue flights from Fort Lauderdale to and New York LaGuardia and Boston.

The retrofit should be nearly done by the end of 2027, covering every JetBlue plane that doesn't have Mint.

BlueFirst tickets are currently on sale for travel dates beginning in December. The cabins will be added to more than 30 routes throughout 2026; you'll start seeing the new seats on flights from JFK to Cancún, Liberia, and San Juan beginning in January. However, even on those inaugural routes, not every flight will have BlueFirst right away (it depends on whether a fitted plane is operating that flight). Just over a dozen planes will have the cabin by the end of this year, with the rest of the fleet following through 2027.

By the end of next year, the retrofit should be nearly done, covering every JetBlue plane that doesn't have Mint. Until then, it's worth double-checking before booking since JetBlue notes BlueFirst may only be available on select flights or dates, and planes can be swapped at a moment’s notice depending on equipment needs and maintenance.

Here are seven cards worth considering alongside the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

For a $95 annual fee, the Venture Rewards also gives you access to Capital One's 15-plus transfer partners, opening up additional redemption opportunities beyond Chase Ultimate Rewards.

Key drawbacks: While the Venture Rewards has a relatively modest annual fee, it still brings your combined annual fees to $890.

You'll also be managing two separate rewards currencies, since Chase Ultimate Rewards points and Capital One miles can't be combined directly. While this opens up more redemption opportunities across different rewards programs, just make sure you're comfortable managing two rewards currencies before committing to both cards.

However, it doesn't offer some of the perks that come with carrying a United credit card, like free checked bags and priority boarding.

After all, the goal isn't necessarily to have more credit cards. It's to make sure the cards you do carry work well together.

#6252. Coffin Corner: How Little Speed Margins Can Lead To Uncontrollable Stalls & Nose-Dives At Such High Altitudes

The 'coffin corner' is the name for a dangerous flight profile in which an aircraft’s low-speed stall threshold and maximum wing speed converge at extreme altitude. As a jet climbs into lower air density, the airspeed required to generate lift increases, raising the stall speed. At the same time, dropping ambient temperatures lower the local speed of sound. At this lofty altitude, a jet pilot can find themselves trapped in a performance bottleneck where flying just a few knots too slow triggers a violent aerodynamic stall, while flying a few knots too fast can send the jet into a dive that will rip the wings off.

Flying in the narrow performance band of the coffin corner, officially known as the 'q-corner,' leaves virtually zero margin for error. Clear-air turbulence, air temperature spikes, or steep banking angles will instantly increase the wing load factor. This pushes the stall speed to dangerous numbers, making the safe speed window precariously small. Overspeeding causes high-speed Mach buffet, wing damage, or nose-down pitching from shockwaves. Dropping under the lower speed threshold triggers an immediate low-speed stall, potentially causing a catastrophic loss of control.

Pilots navigating through this critical phase of flight must apply extremely precise throttle control and subtle pitch adjustments to maintain stable flight. If the plane deviates from the delicate profile, a recovery leaves little option other than cutting power and gently descending into lower, denser air layers to expand the stable speed envelope. The Lockheed U-2 spy plane is a classic example of aerospace design pushing the extreme possibilities of this aerodynamic tightrope, routinely cruising at 70,000 feet (21,336 meters) while flying inside a five-knot window between a stall and midair disintegration.

A jet's wings encounter an aerodynamic conflict as they get closer to the Q-corner. Flying at high altitude induces the coffin corner due to two simultaneous, opposing shifts in atmospheric physics: decreasing air density and decreasing ambient temperature. As an aircraft climbs, these forces dynamically squeeze its safe speed limits from both ends. This situation results in a stationary boundary layer shockwave, chaotic airflow, and Mach buffet, a vibration that can resemble low-speed stalls but is caused by exceeding design parameters rather than insufficient speed.

A wing requires a specific mass of air flowing over it to generate enough lift to support the aircraft's weight. Because the air is thin, the plane must travel at a much faster physical speed, its True Airspeed (TAS), just to achieve the same amount of aerodynamic lift. As altitude increases, the minimum speed required to keep the aircraft flying, or its low-speed stall limit, continually climbs higher.

As the air gets colder with rising altitude, the speed of sound drops. At the same time, air flowing over the curved top of an airplane wing accelerates. If the plane flies too fast, that localized airflow will hit the speed of sound. This shockwave disrupts the air over the wing, causing severe turbulence, a loss of lift, and a dangerous nose-down pitch called 'Mach tuck.'

Since high altitude raises the minimum safe speed and lowers the maximum safe speed, the two boundaries inevitably converge. At an aircraft's aerodynamic ceiling, the margin disappears entirely, trapping the plane in a highly restrictive velocity corner where it can neither speed up nor slow down safely. Inside the coffin corner, the margin to tolerate an Angle of Attack (AoA) change is almost zero.

Pilot decision-making can be further complicated by instrumentation at the coffin apex, as signs of rapid speed, Mach limits, and low-speed stall margins converge. Modern autopilot systems reduce the hazards of overcorrection in this delicate environment by making minute modifications to preserve stability. Still, clear air turbulence (CAT) is invisible and violent. When an airplane hits an updraft or downdraft, the air hits the wing at a sudden, sharp angle. This drastically changes the wing's AoA, sometimes catastrophically.

U-2 spy plane pilots operate under extreme physiological constraints that actively compound spatial disorientation. Cruising at 70,000 feet, the pilots must wear bulky, restrictive full-pressure spacesuits that severely limit peripheral vision, deaden the tactile feedback from the control yoke, and introduce ambient helmet noise that masks critical sounds. Compounding this isolation is the visual void of the stratosphere, where the sky above turns pitch black and the horizon below blurs into a featureless curvature.

Cockpit displays must be used exclusively due to the absence of external visual references. Significant cognitive fatigue results from operating on pure oxygen during missions longer than nine hours. The pilot has very little time and no margin for error to safely determine which side of the coffin corner they have breached in the case of a stall or overspeed occurrence due to weariness and the extremely narrow five-knot cruise window.

Coffin corner hazards in commercial aviation, on the other hand, are mostly caused by abrupt, disorganized shifts from flawless automation to human flying along with false inner-ear perceptions. When a loss of control triggers sudden vertical deceleration or negative G-forces, it can induce an illusion of false pitch change. That is when the brain misinterprets this acceleration as a severe pitch change in the opposite direction, convincing the pilot the aircraft is climbing when it is actually diving.

'Automation shock' can increase this sensory illusion. Because pilots spend nearly all their cruising time monitoring highly reliable systems, an unexpected sensor failure that disables the autopilot can trigger an adrenaline rush and cognitive tunneling. Under this extreme stress, airline pilots can easily become fixated on a single instrument or their deceptive physical sensations, completely filtering out loud stall signals because their brains cannot absorb the reality that their heavy jet is stalling in thin air.

These five airports produce visual illusions at night that range from false horizons to invisible mountains.

A stall is tactile and instantly identifiable at lower elevations. The engine sound dramatically shifts, the nose dips, and the controls become slow. A stall behaves completely differently within the coffin corner at 40,000 feet or above because, despite the thin air, the aircraft is moving at a very high actual airspeed. A pilot's natural reaction is to pull back on the controls if they mistake a low-speed buffet for an overspeed alert. This can quickly deepen a stall past the point of saving if done incorrectly.

A recoverable standstill can turn into a deadly spiral due to spatial disorientation. In the coffin corner, the sensations of a high-altitude loss of control can directly contradict cockpit instrument readings, creating a cognitive mismatch that quickly overloads human limits. The pilot cannot intuitively tell if the vibrations are caused by a low-speed aerodynamic stall or a high-speed Mach buffet. The physical sensations of both hazards feel practically identical in the cockpit.

The Lockheed U-2 purposely operates inside the coffin corner to maintain its extraordinary cruise altitude of 70,000 feet. At this altitude, the difference between a low-speed aerodynamic stall and a deadly high-speed Mach buffet is a mere five to seven knots. The aircraft flies on a continuous aerodynamic knife-edge, where a simple banking maneuver can cause the inner wing to stall from lowering too slowly and the outer wing to break apart by exceeding its critical Mach limit.

U-2 pilots rely solely on micro-precise autopilot stability loops to survive this harsh operational environment. In contrast, Air France Flight 447 represents a commercial airliner forced into the coffin corner by human error after a technical malfunction. Cruising at 35,000 feet (10,668 meters), the Airbus A330 lost its airspeed indications when ice crystals blocked its pitot sensors, causing the autopilot to disconnect automatically.

Disoriented by the sudden manual control takeover in a severe storm, the jet was forced into a hard climb to 38,000 feet (11,582.4 meters) because the pilot unintentionally pulled back on the controls. The aircraft's stall speed was immediately increased, and the flying envelope was slammed shut as a result of this quick rise, losing crucial forward momentum as it entered thinner air.

The crew was unaware that they had caused a high-altitude aerodynamic stall. They trapped the aircraft in an unrecoverable dive, which resulted in a deadly collision with the Atlantic Ocean, by repeatedly pulling back on the side-stick rather than lowering the nose down into thicker air to regain airspeed.

When an aircraft takes off, pilots must make some of the quickest reactionary decisions anyone can make. Only two seconds can make or break the flight

When a U-2 slips over its five-knot cruise margin and enters a high-speed dive, structural breakdown occurs nearly instantly. The U-2, which is designed like an ultra-lightweight motorized glider with a massive wingspan, cannot withstand the tremendous aerodynamic loads or supersonic shockwaves created during a descent. Its long, frail wings will physically twist and fail at speeds somewhat higher than its regular cruise velocity.

In comparison, the Bombardier CRJ200 cargo plane involved in the West Air Europe tragedy was designed with significantly more structural strength. Believing the aircraft was pitching up uncontrollably because of a malfunctioning attitude indicator display, the captain pushed the yoke hard forward. The plane entered an inverted, near-vertical dive from 33,000 feet (10,058.4 meters), draining its altitude in just sixty seconds. Severe disorientation can set in when a steep drop is initiated from high cruise altitudes.

Spatial disorientation is brought on by this abrupt vertical acceleration. The captain's malfunctioning display continued to show a significant rise even though the first officer's instrument panel accurately showed that they were plummeting vertically toward the frozen landscape. The crew was unable to reconcile the contradictory data before terminal impact because they were trapped in the dark and unable to communicate efficiently due to the tremendous gravity forces. Surprisingly, even though the aircraft was approaching the speed of sound, it didn't disintegrate in midair; instead, it only did so when it hit the ground.

#6251. Great Wolf Lodge Coupons: 50% Off This November

Family vacations come in all shapes and sizes, but sometimes, it’s all about the kids. That’s when places like Great Wolf Lodge come in clutch. Between the indoor water parks, arcades, and arts and crafts, they’re designed for keeping bundles of energy entertained…both kids and kids at heart. I’ve been to a Great Wolf Lodge once (in LaGrange, just outside of Atlanta) and had a ball going down those water slides and playing arcade games, even as a kid-free twenty-something.

The family resort chain has more than 20 properties across North America; most are clustered on the East Coast and in the Midwest, though there are a handful out west too. If a family vacation calls and you’re looking for ways to save on the stay, keep reading.

Great news—Great Wolf Lodge's early Black Friday sale has begun! Book by November 15 for access to room rates starting at $89 for stays taken by February 25, 2027. Browse locations here; the coupon code will be added automatically as you check out. Of note, Great Wolf Lodge Ontario is excluded from this promotion, but many others, including locations in Scottsdale, the Poconos, and the Wisconsin Dells, are taking part.

While last-minute discounts do exist, it also pays to plan ahead. Save up to 50% when you book your stay at least 60 days in advance with the Great Wolf Lodge promo code ESAVER. This coupon applies to a range of suite styles, from standard Family Suites to larger themed Wolf Den or KidCabin suites. The longer you stay, the more you’ll save—and Great Wolf recently upped the ante with 30% off one-night stays, 40% off two-night stays, and 50% for three-plus night stays. This offer is ideal for guests looking for a Great Wolf Lodge promo code while planning for fall or winter vacations. Of notes, this offer may not be valid during holiday and blackout periods, and cannot be combined with any other discount or promotional offers.

For more short-term plans, use Great Wolf Lodge’s discount code TRIPLEFUN to take up to 40% off your total stay when staying three nights or longer within 60 days of booking. The length of stay requirements for this Great Wolf Lodge coupon mean you’ll have more time to fully experience all of the lodge activities, from the water park to the ropes course and arcade. Of note, Great Wolf Lodge Niagara is excluded from the deal.

If you’re planning a weekend trip (or a shorter mid-week trip!), use promo code MOREFUN to save 30% on two-night bookings for stays within 60 days of purchase. Again, this code is good for the rest of the year, so keep it tucked in the back of your mind if you’ve got a later-in-the-year trip brewing.

Special discounted rates on Great Wolf Lodge day passes are available for military members (active, retired, and veteran), teachers, fire and emergency medical service personnel, medical providers, nurses, 911 dispatchers, police, government employees, and correctional officers looking for a respite. If you work in one of these professions, use the Great Wolf Lodge discount code WPHEROES to access reduced pricing on stays. This code is good through the end of 2028, and you’ll need to verify your status using ID.me.

Grandparents and older parents can get in on the fun with exclusive savings for guests aged 65 and older when using the promo code SENIORS. Proof of age is required at check-in to validate this Great Wolf Lodge discount code. More good news: It’s often combinable with other lodge perks to maximize savings when traveling with the whole family. Great Wolf Lodge Niagara is excluded from this deal.

Members of AAA, AARP, or other vehicle clubs can also save on lodge bookings. Enter your membership details to activate the Great Wolf Lodge AAA discount or Great Wolf Lodge AARP discount. Plan to bring your card with you, as membership cards must also be presented upon arrival. Right now, there is a promo code DRIVER that takes up to 30% off your bill.

One other reliable way to save: Join the Voyagers Club for free to earn points and exclusive members-only deals. Members get early access to Great Wolf Lodge promotion code releases and seasonal sales. They’ll also earn Voyagers Points for money spent at the lodge, which can be redeemed for future stays or on-site amenities.

You'll get a point for every $10 spent on bookings, package add-ons, cabanas, ancillary purchases like late checkout, and on-site spending charged to the suite, including food and retail. Points are not earned on any alcohol purchases, taxes, gratuities, fees, or on-site purchases not charged to the suite. You can check your points balance at any time in your Great Wolf profile, and redeem them by booking directly on greatwolf.com while logged into your account.

Having trouble with a promo code? There are a few things you can do to fix that. First, double check that the code is spelled correctly, with no extra spaces or typos. If all looks good, check the details of the promo code to ensure it's still active and hasn't expired. Some discount codes exclude certain locations, so make sure your booking meets any necessary criteria to qualify. If everything looks good and your Great Wolf Lodge promo code still isn't working, clear your browser's cache and give the page a refresh. When in doubt, contact the brand's customer service team for help (which varies by location).

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. #6250. Aeromexico Adds New U.S. Routes, Flights

Aeromexico is again expanding its footprint in the U.S. with assistance from longtime partner Delta.

The carrier announced Monday that it will connect Mexico City with Nashville, Tennessee, New Orleans, and San Juan, Puerto Rico. None of the three cities currently has nonstop service to the Mexican capital.

All three connections will operate four times weekly. Service to Nashville will launch first, on June 13, 2027, followed by New Orleans on June 17 and San Juan on June 24.

Flights to Nashville and New Orleans will use Embraer E190 aircraft with 99 seats. For the route to San Juan, the airline will operate Boeing 737 MAX 8s with 166 seats.

Aeromexico will also launch a second daily service between Mexico City and Austin, Texas, on June 3.

“The addition of Nashville, New Orleans, and San Juan to our network will allow us to provide more connectivity options, bringing our customers closer to destinations known for their unique identity and remarkable attractions,” Giancarlo Mulinelli, senior vice president of global sales at Aeromexico, said in a news release. “Together with Delta, we continue to open markets and create more opportunities that strengthen tourism and ties between Mexico and the United States.”

Last month, the partners announced new routes from Mexico City to Orange County, California, Fort Lauderdale, Florida, and Portland, Oregon.

#6249. The Best Ski Resorts in Europe: 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards

For our 39th annual Readers’ Choice Awards, survey voters weighed in on their favorite ski resorts in Europe. Swiss resorts earned four of the top five spots, with Verbier claiming the number one ranking for the second consecutive year. Italy’s Olympic spotlight helped it land an unprecedented five resorts on the list. The tiny ski resort of Gudauri in Georgia’s Caucasus Mountains made its debut in the rankings—proof that readers are venturing further afield for fresh tracks. Here are the ski resorts that you loved most, for both their diversity of terrain, excellent après ski scenes, and exceptional hotels.

The Caucasus Mountains may not have the cachet of the Alps or the Rockies, but there are plenty of reasons to make the journey to ski in Georgia. The ski passes are a bargain. The slopes are uncrowded. And the food rivals anything you’ll have in France or Italy. Gudauri, the country’s premier ski resort has just over 50 miles of groomed trails, plus freeriding opportunities. There’s a mom-and-pop vibe, with stalls at the base of the mountain selling wool-knit socks, and churchkhela, candle-like strings of nuts encased in a wax-like, grape juice. Travel Bar and La Suite are the main après ski spots (be warned, the local brandy, chacha, is like rocket fuel). Plan an early on-slope lunch at Cafe Vitamin, where you can dig into traditional dishes like khachapuri, molten cheese (often topped with an egg) baked into a shallow bread bowl.

Where to stay: Ski-in/ski-out Gudauri Lodge has 171 rooms across five categories and a sprawling open-air hot tub. Ati Ambavi is a boutique hotel with room decor inspired by cultural icons like Georgian-American ballet master George Balanchine and Georgian artist Niko Pirosmani. The Rooms Kazbegi hotel is a 40-minute drive from the ski resort but its mountain views, delicious Georgian restaurant, and hip vibe are worth the commute.

Stats: There are 14 lifts for nearly 50 miles of runs. One-day lift ticket from $27.

Located on the Italian side of the Matterhorn massif, the high-altitude ski resort of Cervinia is linked with the Swiss resort of Zermatt. The combined terrain is vast, making it possible to log serious mileage without repeating a run all day. The majority of slopes are geared toward beginners and intermediates and the on-piste dining options are exceptional. Many skiers cross the border just to lunch on pasta all'Amatriciana and sip Bombardinos (an Italian riff on eggnog). Cervino The One is a new cableway project connecting Breuil-Cervinia with Plateau Rosa/Testa Grigia in just over 15 minutes. The modern two-section 3S gondola by Leitner includes a mid-station at Plan Maison.

Where to stay: Stylish apartments at Saint Hubertus Resort have modern kitchens, marble bathrooms, and stone living rooms with fireplaces. The team at five-star Hermitage Hotel & Spa can arrange adventures ranging from snowshoeing to heliskiing.

Stats: There are 19 lifts for 72 runs. One-day lift ticket from $52; on the Ikon pass.

Located on the sunnier, Italian side of Mont Blanc, Courmayeur attracts both dedicated skiers and unapologetic sybarites who prefer to sip Aperol spritzes on terraces by day and dine on gourmet meals at night. The Skyway Monte Bianco cable car whisks skiers across the Italian-French border where they can test their mettle on 11-plus miles of spectacular off-piste slopes, including the bucket-list glacial run of the Vallée Blanche in Chamonix. The resort’s modernized snowmaking system guarantees snow on over 8o percent of the slopes, every day of the season. After the pistes close, the Courmayeur Cable Car continues running until midnight so you can dine at mountain-top restaurants like LaChaumière. You can also experience the adventure of a snowmobile climb to reach fancy alpine huts like Rifugio Monte Bianco.

Where to stay: Auberge de la Maison is the epitome of alpine romance. Most rooms have panoramic views of Mont Blanc and the spa features unique alpine therapies such as a hay bio-sauna.

Stats: One-day lift ticket from $83; there are 18 lifts for 33 trails.

When an Egyptian billionaire opened five-star The Chedi Andermatt hotel (more on that later) in 2013, it turned a relatively unknown ski area tucked between Zermatt and St. Moritz into an international ski destination. The largest ski area in the heart of Switzerland has such varied and vast terrain you never have to repeat a run. Gemsstock is a steep, free-riding playground while neighboring Nätschen is laced with cruise-y runs. And if you want something more mellow, you can easily link to the family-friendly slopes of Sedrun. When your legs get tired from all the skiing, the Matterhorn Gotthard railway (also included in the ticket) will take you back to Andermatt. This season, Andermatt-Sedrun will open two new chairlifts, the Val Val-Calmut and Val Val-Cuolm, doubling capacity to 2,400 skiers per hour. The culinary scene is more impressive than ever now that Swiss star chef Andres Caminada has opened an outpost of his IGNIV restaurant concept in Andermatt’s Reuss district.

Where to stay: The extravagant Chedi Andermatt has 123 spacious rooms and suites all boasting fireplaces, Hästens mattresses, and large balconies. Set aside plenty of time to soak in the spa’s hydrotherapy zone and indulge in the 16-foot-high, glass-walled, climate-controlled Cheese Tower or The Japanese, the hotel’s Michelin-star Japanese restaurant.|

Stats: Average price for a one-day lift ticket is $120; the Andermatt-Sedrun-Disentis ski region comprises 33 lifts for 93 marked pistes; on the Epic Pass.

Located on the ridge between Tuscany and Emilia-Romagna, Abetone is Central Italy’s largest ski region. Many call it Florence’s secret ski resort as it’s just a 90-minute drive from the city. The family-friendly resort is made up of four interconnected valleys. Local ski champ Zeno Colò designed a handful of runs including the “Zeno” slopes in the Valley of Luce. There’s also a dedicated Nordic skiing area. The slopes are rarely crowded, especially in the afternoons, which are dedicated to long leisurely lunches at rifugios like La Selletta and Monte Gomito.

Where to stay: Val di Luce Spa Resort has spacious family suites that sleep four to six, many with well-equipped kitchens. The spa is a highlight with a pool housed in a Louvre-like glass pyramid so you can gaze at the starry night sky.

Stats: There are 17 lifts for just over 30 miles of runs. One-day lift ticket from $60.

Perched at 5,950 feet, this remote ski town in Lombardy is nicknamed “Little Tibet.” Its four, high-altitude snowparks served as the Winter Olympic stage for freestyle skiing and snowboarding. And its party scene is just as rowdy as its terrain. Set at the base of the Carosello 3000 cable car beneath a huge circus tent, Stalet is an après ski institution known for its crazy costumes, tabletop dancing, and DJ sets. On the Mottolino slopes, Camanel di Planon is an old-school mountain hut with a panoramic terrace and daily 1p.m. music-and-dance show. The best way to arrive at Milky’s Disco Club is via a copper slide at the entrance (stairs are also an option). Party nights are often themed and costumes are highly recommended.

Where to stay: Hotel Spöl is a five-star, adults-only property in Valtellina with a new longevity-focused spa that offers therapies like cryo and molecular hydrogen boosters.

Stats: There are 32 lifts for 78 runs. One-day lift ticket from $74.

Zermatt, surrounded by the Alps’ tallest peaks, has 223 miles of runs in four huge ski areas—some at an altitude of over 10,000 feet, so snow here lingers well beyond the winter season. This enchanting, alpine village lies at the foot of the Matterhorn, Switzerland's most famous mountain, and has plenty of modern touches, like its swanky après-ski diversions and state-of-the-art lift system, recently enhanced this season with the new 6-seater Patrullarve chairlift. Horse-drawn sleighs are the preferred choice of transportation in the car-free village. On the slopes, be sure to stop for the burger at Chez Vrony (reservations a must) and a glass of bubbles at the tiny Champagne bar at the end of the Sunnega run. The new Matterhorn Glacier Ride II now links the entire stretch between Zermatt and Cervinia by cable car, connecting the Matterhorn Glacier Paradise mountain station with the Testa Grigia valley station. Cervino The One is an ambitious new cableway project on the Italian side, connecting Breuil-Cervinia with Plateau Rosa/Testa Grigia in just over 15 minutes.

Where to stay: Grand dame Mont Cervin Palace and modern-luxe Schweizerhof Zermatt, both offer prime central locations and every imaginable amenity. Just above the village, slope-side CERVO Mountain Resort has an ashram-inspired spa with an expansive network of outdoor pools, saunas, and soaking tubs.Riffelalp Resort is another favorite located directly on the slopes, and the Omnia is beautifully nestled into the mountains just above the village.

Stats: There are 55 lifts for 147 runs. One-day lift ticket from $87; on the Ikon Pass.

Poised on a south-facing mountain plateau, Alpe d'Huez is aptly nicknamed “Island in the Sun,” averaging 300 days of sunshine per year. This vast ski area connects several charming villages—Huez, Vaujany, Oz-en-Oisans, Auris-en-Oisans, and Villard-Reculas—and contains terrain to satisfy every skier, from cruisey blues to 10-mile-long La Sarenne, the lengthiest black diamond run in France. Its high elevation—Pic Blanc summit reaches 10,925 feet—also makes it reliably snow sure. On-mountain restaurants, like L'Alpette Chez Passoud, served made-from-scratch regional dishes like tartiflette. And there’s a lively après ski scene anchored by iconic party spot La Folie Douce. Each March, electronic music festival Tomorrowland, takes over the slopes.

Where to stay: Club Med’s all-inclusive ski packages offer great value and the brand’s Alpe d'Huez location is perched at 6,100 feet, delivering ski-in/ski-out access and sensational views. The 5-star Daria-1 Nor hotel, part of the French Les Étincelles Collection, offers direct access to the Alpe Express gondola, and its spa is the ultimate sanctuary for recovery with a hammam, contrast therapy, and a Himalayan salt wall. Hotel Pic Blanc has cozy chalet vibes and a fantastic restaurant.

Stats: There are 84 lifts for 111 runs. One-day lift ticket from $65.

With three nearby airports—Munich, Salzburg, and Innsbruck—Kitzbühel is easily Austria’s most popular holiday resort. The legendary alpine sports town has it all: posh hotels, a picturesque 750-year-old town center, a lively après-ski scene along quaint, cobblestone streets, and unsurpassed skiing that includes 11 renowned ski schools and the most demanding course on the World Cup circuit. With more than 60 mountain huts and restaurants, there are plenty of delicious options to refuel, or lounge leisurely over lunch on the slopes. The resort also has a stellar line-up of winter events, including the Sound Escape music festival (December 11 -12, 2026) and the Bendura Bank Snow Polo World Cup (Jan. 15-17, 2027).

Where to stay: Hotel Schloss Lebenberg, a medieval hillside castle overlooking the village that earns high marks for its stellar service, dining room, and ornate, Gothic-style décor. For affordability and convenience, check out the Henri boutique hotel by the train station.

Stats: 58 lifts for 96 runs covering 145 miles. One-day lift tickets average $92; on the Ikon Pass.

Megève may not have the haute party scene of, say, St. Moritz, or the breadth of sporty-centric Courchevel, but it still has plenty to tout. Two ski areas are covered with nearly 250 miles of runs linked by state-of-the-art cable cars. Skiers can choose from 50-plus on-mountain restaurants, like the excellent La Ferme de Mon Père. A charming, car-free city center featuring an open-air ice rink, cobbled streets, horse-drawn sleighs, as well as a number of smart boutiques makes Megève a family favorite.

Where to stay: The resort's primary patrons—streams of well-heeled Parisians looking to escape the city—reserve rooms at Relais & Châteaux Flocons de Sel, or the Les Fermes de Marie, a tiny mountain chalet where the rooms have fur throws, wood-beamed ceilings, and stone accent walls. Four Seasons Hotel Megève and 12-room Le Chalet, from Zannier Hotels, both offer five-star service.

Stats: There are 112 lifts for nearly 250 runs for the Évasion Mont-Blanc ski area. One-day lift tickets from $60. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited Pass starts at $116 and includes 10 ski areas and nearly 450 miles of slopes across three countries; on the Mountain Collective Pass.

Val Thorens is a resort of superlatives. Europe’s highest ski resort offers one of the continent’s longest ski seasons, running from November 21, 2026, to May 2, 2027, and is part of Les 3 Vallées, the world’s largest linked ski area, with more than 370 miles of runs. This winter, the resort is expanding its appeal with new dining spots, thrilling off-slope activities and a fresh high-altitude experience. At Caron 3200, perched at 10,498 feet, visitors can embark on a virtual-reality ascent of Everest, immersing themselves in the journey to the world’s highest summit without leaving the Alps. For those seeking a different kind of adrenaline rush, the resort is introducing Mountain Kart Xperience, while the Cosmojet toboggan run offers three miles of exhilarating downhill fun. The Bee zipline adds another dose of adventure, soaring 5,905 feet above the slopes. The dining scene is also evolving: Le Bouchon Alpin brings a taste of Lyonnais and Savoyard classics, Le Neva serves contemporary French cuisine inspired by seasonal ingredients, and Zig Zag Café opens as the resort’s first dedicated coffee shop. Meanwhile, the international freeride spotlight returns to Val Thorens from January 25 to 30, 2027, when the Freeride World Tour brings the world’s best skiers and snowboarders to its dramatic high-mountain terrain. The après ski scene has long been legendary, known for party institutions like La Folie Douce and low-key gathering spots such as La Timbale, a tapas bar in the heart of the village.

Where to stay: Five-star Hótel Pashmina for the outdoor spa with stunning mountain views.

Stats: 25 lifts for 93 miles of pistes. One-day lift ticket for Val Thorens starting at $77. One-day lift ticket for the Three Valleys $98; on the Epic Pass.

The oldest winter holiday resort in the world is as elegant and exclusive as it gets. As if St. Moritz wasn't already blessed enough at nearly 6,000 feet above sea level, the sun shines 322 days a year, pairing with the dry air for what’s known as a “Champagne climate.” But it’s the world-class hotels and restaurants, chic shopping, and excellent skiing on- and off-piste that draw celebrities and royalty alike. The iconic alpine city is equally famous for its unique events on the frozen lake St. Moritz: the Snow Polo World Cup St. Moritz, the White Turf horse racing and the ICE car show. The restaurant scene has never been more varied, from cult Italian franchise Crazy Pizza and Greek hotspot Neora at the Grand Hotel des Bains Kempinski St. Moritz to Beefbar at Grace La Margna.

Where to stay: A room in the Serlas Wing at alpine grand dame Badrutt's Palace Hotel, which has been indulging A-listers since 1896, or at the Kulm Hotel—one of our Gold List favorites—can do no wrong.

Stats: There are 58 lifts for 88 runs. One-day lift tickets range from $45 to $100; on the Ikon Pass.

Lech Zürs may lack the bling of areas like St. Moritz and Cortina d’Ampezzo, but that’s part of its charm. Behind traditional farmhouse facades you’ll find chic, family-run boutiques, art galleries, and stylish hotels and chalets. The village of 1,600 may be tiny, but it boasts one of the highest density of award-winning restaurants in the world (Rote Wand Chef’s Table at Rote Wand Gourmet Hotel is a must). And of course there’s the draw of its excellent snowfall and the famed White Ring, a circuit of nearly 14 miles that links Lech, Zürs, Zug, and Oberlech. Two modern cable cars make the slopes even more accessible.

Where to stay: Five-star Hotel Almhof Schneider is the epitome of alpine elegance, with a serious art collection, serene spa, and a 25,000-bottle wine cellar. The family behind the property also recently opened two, design-centric chalets, Haus W and Chalet Sonnenhof. Boutique stay Hotel Kristiania was originally established by Olympic skier Othmar Schneider, and his family continues the hotel’s legacy of hospitality. The Yurt, a salon-inspired après bar within a Kyrgyz-style tent, takes up residency on the hotel grounds this season.

Stats: Part of the Arlberg, Austria’s largest inter-linked ski area, 85 lifts and cable cars can access more than 180 miles of marked slopes and 120-plus miles of backcountry runs. One-day lift ticket from $95; on the Epic Pass.

Chamonix-Mont Blanc’s expansive backcountry and gnarly terrain make it a bucket-list destination for serious skiers. Host to the first winter Olympics in 1924, the pedestrian-friendly town oozes alpine charm and, despite the mountain’s extreme reputation, there are plenty of beginner and intermediate runs. Riding the Aiguille du Midi, the highest cable car in Western Europe is a must simply for the views. From the top, experienced skiers can schuss down the legendary Vallée Blanche, 12.4-mile glacier descent in the heart of Mont-Blanc Massif. A guide is essential for the descent and Chamonix has the world’s oldest and largest guiding organization. The eclectic dining scene draws on flavors from around the world. Essential reservations include Mumma, which specializes in Asian and South American fusion cuisine, and Yumidori, a Japanese spot helmed by a sushi world champ. Restaurant Le 3842, one of the highest restaurants in Europe, serves a three-course lunch atop the Aiguille du Midi.

Where to stay: La Folie Douce Hotel has a hip vibe, a lively après scene and an unbeatable location in the heart of Chamonix, with a ski lift steps from the front door. For over-the-top luxury, book a stay at Hameau Albert 1er. The five-star hotel has 33 rooms, two suites and two stand-alone chalets and a Michelin-star restaurant. Le Collectionist’s portfolio of luxury chalets range from three to 12 bedrooms.

Stats: There are 82 lifts for 91 runs. One-day lift ticket from $55; on the Ikon Pass and Mountain Collective Pass. The Mont-Blanc Unlimited Pass starts at $85 and includes 10 ski areas and nearly 450 miles of slopes across three countries.

#6248. All Nippon Airways (ANA) New 777 First & Business Class: Which Routes Get Them?

In 2019, Japanese Star Alliance carrier All Nippon Airways (ANA) launched an all-new first and business class product. In this post, I’d like to take an updated look at ANA’s progress with installing these new cabins, along with which routes currently consistently feature this product.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class and business class products are truly spectacular. ANA has always had incredible service, and now the airline has a hard product to match.

All Nippon Airways’ new first class, known as “The Suite,” is phenomenal. The hard product as such doesn’t look that amazing, but it’s a huge improvement over the old product. First class has eight very comfortable suites, each of which is functionally designed and private. Personally I consider this to be among the world’s best first class products, thanks largely to ANA’s top notch soft product.

All Nippon Airways’ new business class, known as “The Room,” is really what’s most revolutionary. The seats have doors and an unreal amount of personal space. I consider this to be one of the world’s best business class products, along with Qatar Airways’ Qsuites and Japan Airlines’ A350 business class.

While there are certain markets where All Nippon Airways consistently offers the new cabins, we have seen some variance. So let me share the basics of how many ANA 777s have the new cabins, how you can tell if your flight features the new cabins, and finally which routes currently feature the new cabins (though of course that’s subject to change).

All Nippon Airways has 13 Boeing 777-300ERs in its fleet. 10 of the 13 jets currently feature the new cabins, meaning that ~77% of ANA’s 777-300ERs have the new first and business class. Six of these planes have been delivered to the airline since 2019, with the new cabins, while four 777-300ERs have been reconfigured with the new cabins (these planes are 10+ years old).

Unfortunately ANA doesn’t have concrete plans to reconfigure the remaining 777-300ERs, so don’t expect this product’s footprint to grow much for the time being. ANA is expected to eventually take delivery of new 777-9s, which will likely feature this product (or something even better), though that’s still potentially years down the road.

If you want to track registration codes, the following 10 Boeing 777-300ERs feature the new cabins:

And in the interest of being thorough, here are the three Boeing 777-300ERs that feature the old cabins:

It’s obviously frustrating to have a fleet of just 13 planes, and not reconfigure three of them, especially when it has been seven years. What’s the explanation for this? Keep in mind that the 777X has been delayed by around seven years now.

My guess is that ANA had intended to reconfigure 10 planes and retire the other three, and signed contracts based on that. Then with the never-ending 777X delays, the airline decided to keep those jets around, and maybe it just proved too complicated or costly to backtrack on that. At least that’s my best guess.

You can tell whether or not your flight is scheduled to feature All Nippon Airways’ new cabins just by looking at the seat map. The easiest way to tell is to look at the business class seat map:

If you’re on ANA’s website and a flight is scheduled to be operated with the new cabins, you’ll also see the prominent display of “THE SUITE” for first class and “THE ROOM” for business class.

Another method to check without using ANA’s website is to instead go to Google Flights. Just search a business class flight on an ANA 777. When you look at the flight options, if a flight shows as having an “Individual suite,” then that’s the new business class.

Meanwhile if it shows as having a “Lie flat seat,” then that’s the old business class.

Again, it’s only select Boeing 777-300ERs that have these cabins. You won’t find these cabins on other aircraft, including 787s, A380s, etc. However:

Here are the routes that are typically currently operated by the new All Nippon Airways Boeing 777-300ERs:

In other words, as it stands, all flights to London and New York are supposed to feature the new cabins. Meanwhile flights to Chicago and San Francisco all alternate between new and old configurations, so you’ll want to check the seat map. That means there are no routes that are exclusively operated by 777s with the old cabins.

In terms of the rest of the United States route network, Houston (IAH), Los Angeles (LAX), Seattle (SEA), and Washington (IAD), are served by 787s. There’s always the chance for last minute aircraft swaps, and airlines do tweak their schedules over time.

All Nippon Airways introduced a phenomenal new first and business class in 2019, and the airline has rolled this out to ~77% of its 777-300ER fleet (though no additional retrofits have happened in the past several years).

For the current upcoming schedule, you can expect the new cabins to be offered on all flights to London and New York, as well as on select flights to Chicago and San Francisco. While you’ll always want to check the seat map for changes or aircraft swaps, that’s the current plan.

#6247. Alaska, Hawaiian Pilot MECs Approve Tentative Joint Contract

Pilots at Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines are one step closer to a deal that will bring both work groups together under a single labor contract.

ALPA announced Wednesday that its Alaska and Hawaiian master executive councils unanimously approved a tentative agreement on a joint collective bargaining compact. The two councils had been negotiating since February 2025.

The proposed agreement will now go before the combined membership for a ratification vote.

Details of the agreement were not immediately available to the public.

Union officials said they worked to address the priorities of both work groups and have established a “contractual foundation for their future as a combined workforce.”

“This TA is the result of more than 600 days of challenging negotiations, countless hours of work by our volunteers, and an unwavering commitment to the pilots we represent,” Drew Coyle, the Alaska MEC chair, said in a statement. “Our Joint Negotiating Committee remained focused on the priorities of both pilot groups while working through some of the most complex issues facing our combined membership. Nothing about this process was easy. Now it’s our pilots’ turn to review the agreement, ask the tough questions, and decide whether it meets their expectations.”

Ratification voting starts Dec. 1 and closes Dec. 22.

Alaska and Hawaiian merged in 2024 and received a single operating certificate from the FAA in 2025. This effectively transformed Hawaiian from an independent airline to a brand under Alaska Air Group. Alaska has pledged to maintain Hawaiian’s brand identity, and Hawaiian retains a separate corporate leadership based in Honolulu.

The two brands have continued to integrate however, with Alaska now making use of long-haul aircraft originally owned by Hawaiian. Earlier this year, Alaska implemented a single passenger service system.

#6246. Why Business Class Suites With Doors Need Additional Aircraft Safety Certification

Business class suite doors therefore need extensive additional safety certification to satisfy the demands of global safety authorities. From 16g crash testing to strict 90-second emergency egress mandates, introducing doors into the cabin requires special exemptions, meticulous testing, and regulatory approvals that frequently lag behind the delivery of the aircraft itself.

Aviation regulators once evaluated premium cabin seating primarily through the lens of traditional structural integrity, restraint systems, and standard evacuation pathways. Traditional open lie-flat business class seats presented straightforward compliance paths because flight attendants and evacuating passengers had clear, unobstructed lines of sight and immediate access to aisles. When manufacturers began designing suites with doors, however, these established certification frameworks proved insufficient to address the new variables introduced by partitioned personal spaces.

The core regulatory concern centered on emergency evacuation under worst-case conditions. According to Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) mandates, any commercial aircraft must be capable of a full evacuation within 90 seconds in total darkness, with half of the emergency exits blocked and amid simulated passenger panic. A closed or jammed sliding door at the start of an emergency could potentially impede a disoriented or panicked passenger from exiting their suite. Consequently, regulators need to be able to see extensive documentation and demonstration proving that a suite door's design, latching mechanism, and breakaway features will not meaningfully delay egress.

Furthermore, cabin doors are governed by strict regulatory classifications, as detailed by Sofema Aviation. Because standard airworthiness rules did not anticipate partial-height sliding doors dividing passenger seats from exit paths, airlines and seat manufacturers must regularly apply for regulatory exemptions or special conditions. These tailored requirements impose rigorous oversight on how doors operate, so that the pursuit of luxury never compromises baseline aviation safety.

Basic egress clearance is just the beginning, as suite doors need to withstand extreme forces and operational stress during flight to get certification. Every premium seat model incorporating a door is subjected to punishing dynamic 16g sled tests, which simulate the immense G-forces of a survivable crash landing. During these tests, the door structure, locking pins, and track mechanisms need to remain intact. This is to show that structural flexing of the airframe does not jam the door shut and trap a passenger inside their suite during an emergency.

In addition to crash dynamics, modern cabin engineering also must account for rapid decompression and airflow management. As highlighted in Simple Flying analysis, tightly sealed suite doors can alter cabin pressure equalization and oxygen mask deployment patterns during a rapid decompression event. Regulators need to see proof that air can flow freely between the enclosed suite and the main cabin volume so that passengers are not starved of supplemental oxygen or subjected to dangerous pressure differentials if hull integrity is compromised at altitude.

The rigorous engineering demands mean that seat development cycles are frequently prolonged. When Qatar Airways partnered with Adient to develop the Ascent seat for its 787-9 fleet, achieving regulatory compliance for the sliding door mechanism contributed significantly to a two-year program delay, culminating in FAA certification being completed in January 2021.

A closer look at what is causing frustration among passengers today, and examining the nuances to see why flying is actually better now than ever.

Even after a suite door successfully passes structural crash tests and evacuation trials, its operational use is still heavily restricted during critical phases of flight. FAA exemption documents and cabin safety guidelines dictate that suite doors must be locked in the open position during taxi, takeoff, and landing (TTL). The reason is that flight attendants need to have an unobstructed view of all seated passengers and all exit pathways should be entirely clear during the most statistically vulnerable phases of flight.

Suite door approvals involve complex human-factors testing and specialized evacuation modeling, so the certification process frequently lags behind the delivery of the aircraft itself. This regulatory timing gap has created a notable phenomenon across major global carriers where airlines take delivery of brand-new aircraft equipped with suite doors, only to fly them with the doors locked open for months while waiting for final paperwork to clear.

United’s new Polaris suites debut on 787-9s with locked doors due to certification delays, echoing a similar issue faced by American Airlines.

Airlines mitigate these expectations through flexible booking disclaimers and proactive notifications. For carriers undergoing fleet retrofits or introducing new interior designs, such as United's phased Polaris rollouts or American's widebody cabin updates, operational transparency helps prevent backlash from frequent flyers who book specifically for the enclosed suite experience. As regulatory bodies become more familiar with partial-height sliding doors, manufacturers are streamlining early certification filing processes to minimize the gap between aircraft entry-into-service and full door activation.

Ultimately, the rigorous certification path required for business class suite doors is just one of many areas that can be pointed to that show commercial aviation prioritizes safety above all else. What appears to the passenger as a simple sliding partition is, in the eyes of regulators, a critical evacuation variable that needs its due process, otherwise known as an exhaustive engineering verification.

The necessity for additional aircraft safety certification on business class suites with doors is just one part of the constant tension between passenger luxury and rigorous regulatory oversight. Turning an open cabin into a network of private suites means working through complex 16g crash dynamics, rapid decompression airflow standards, and strict 90-second emergency evacuation mandates.

JSX is bringing its popular semi-private flights to Beantown.

The boutique air carrier plans to begin flying from Boston this winter, JSX said this week. The company's service will be based out of the nearby Laurence G. Hanscom Field (BED) in the town of Bedford, Massachusetts.

The Boston service will launch with a route to New York City on Feb. 8, followed by flights to Miami-Opa Locka Executive Airport (OPF) in Florida beginning on Feb. 11.

More: JSX eyes more turboprops and new mountain routes after strong passenger response

JSX will operate four daily flights between Boston and New York from Monday through Friday, with two flights on Saturday and three on Sunday. The Miami service will run once per day five times a week: Monday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

Notably, JSX did not specify which New York airport would host the Boston flights. A spokesperson did not immediately answer TPG’s request for further details. JSX typically flies to New York’s Teterboro Airport (TEB) and Westchester County Airport (HPN), although various restrictions set by the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey mean that JSX cannot publicly promote TEB as a destination.

Because of those restrictions, anyone looking to fly to or from New York has to sign up for the free Club JSX program, which offers rewards and has no minimum spending or flying requirements. Passengers can also earn United MileagePlus miles under a partnership between the two companies.

The carrier will use its Embraer E145 aircraft on both routes, which can seat up to 30 passengers in a 1-1 configuration. Fares start at $199 one-way between Boston and New York, with one-way flights between Boston and Miami starting at $599.

Club JSX: Earn rewards and fly in comfort with JSX’s new loyalty program

“Greater Boston represents an exciting new chapter for JSX, marking our first entry into Massachusetts and an important milestone in the continued expansion of our East Coast network,” JSX CEO Alex Wilcox said in a statement.

“As one of the nation's leading centers for business, innovation, and higher education, Greater Boston is a natural fit for our unique approach to flying,” he added.

JSX operates as a “hop-on charter” service, which essentially operates private charter flights that anyone can buy a seat on. It means that JSX flights operate more like private flights than commercial, using posh private Fixed-Base Operators (FBOs) instead of public airport terminals and allowing passengers to venture from curb to seat in just 20 minutes.

The flight experience itself is equally luxurious with no middle seats, lots of legroom, Starlink Wi-Fi, complimentary snacks and drinks and checked luggage that’s returned right at the side of the plane. Overall, the service pitches the idea of private jet convenience for a fraction of the cost.

The public charter service — which does not bill itself as an “airline,” due to different regulations between charter carriers and public airlines — operates out of 29 airports across the U.S. and Mexico. Although private jet passengers typically bypass TSA screening, JSX implemented a more thorough in-house screening process in 2025 to address security concerns.

Still, the process is remarkably quicker than going through the public terminal, making JSX an appealing option for those looking to skip the hassle of a regular flight.

JSX's flights from Boston are already on sale, with service scheduled to start in February.

With the entry to New England, JSX adds its 29th city, and brings its own entry to the competitive business of moving premium travelers between Boston and New York.
